Cellular angiofibroma of the female geni.normalized_text: Cellular angiofibroma of the female genital tract
Cellular angiofibroma of the female geni.description: A rare benign, usually well-circumscribed mesenchymal tumor that occurs most often in the vulvovaginal region but can arise in the cervix or pelvis. It contains bland spindle cells, collagen, and characteristic prominent hyalinized blood vessels.

Angiomyofibroblastoma.description: A benign mesenchymal tumor of the lower female genital tract, usually occurring as a small, slow-growing, sharply circumscribed vulvovaginal or cervical mass. Microscopically it contains stromal spindle or epithelioid cells clustered around numerous thin-walled blood vessels.

Aggressive angiomyxoma (deep angiomyxoma.description: A rare locally infiltrative benign-to-low-grade mesenchymal tumor affecting the pelvis, perineum, vulva, or vagina, typically in women of reproductive age. It is often myxoid and vascular and may show a swirling internal pattern on MRI.

Splenic infarction.description: Ischemic necrosis of splenic tissue, usually caused by arterial embolism, thrombosis, hypercoagulability, hematologic disease, trauma, or vasculitis. Imaging commonly shows peripheral wedge-shaped hypoechoic and nonenhancing splenic areas with reduced vascular flow.

Splenic abscesses or microabscesses.description: Localized infectious collections in the spleen caused by bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, or parasitic infection. They may appear as multiple hypoechoic lesions on ultrasound and focal lesions on MRI.

Splenic lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can involve the spleen as diffuse enlargement, multiple hypoechoic nodules, or focal masses. It may occur as part of systemic Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Splenic sarcoidosis.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that can involve the spleen, producing multiple small hypoechoic nodules that are often relatively hypointense on MRI.

Splenic hydatid disease.description: Hydatid disease is infection by Echinococcus species, endemic in parts of Spain. Splenic involvement is uncommon and typically produces cystic lesions, sometimes with daughter cysts, membranes, or calcified walls.

Hepatic fascioliasis (Fasciola hepatica.description: A parasitic liver infection caused by the liver fluke Fasciola hepatica, which is endemic in parts of Spain. During the hepatic migratory phase it can produce clustered, irregular hypodense liver lesions or inflammatory masses on CT.

Hepatic hydatid disease (cystic echinoco.description: A zoonotic infection caused by Echinococcus granulosus that commonly affects the liver and is endemic in Mediterranean areas, including Spain. It may appear as a hepatic cystic mass with internal daughter cysts, membranes, calcification, or complicated inflammatory changes.

Hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor of the liver, usually arising in the setting of cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B or C infection, alcohol-associated liver disease, or other chronic liver disorders. It can present as a large heterogeneous liver mass with necrosis and satellite nodules.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON).description: A mitochondrial inherited optic neuropathy causing subacute, usually painless central visual loss and progressive optic-nerve atrophy, often affecting both eyes.

Multiple sclerosis-associated optic neur.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause optic neuritis, optic-nerve atrophy, and lesions in the brain and spinal cord.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy, commonly associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, characterized by severe optic neuritis and myelitis that may produce persistent optic atrophy.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder that can cause unilateral or bilateral optic neuritis, myelitis, and brain lesions; residual optic atrophy may occur after optic neuritis.

Harding syndrome (LHON with multiple scl.normalized_text: Harding syndrome (LHON with multiple sclerosis-like demyelinating disease)
Harding syndrome (LHON with multiple scl.description: A rare overlap syndrome in which a patient with a mitochondrial LHON mutation develops optic neuropathy together with multiple-sclerosis-like central nervous system demyelination.

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degener.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder caused by pathogenic ATP7B variants, resulting in impaired biliary copper excretion and toxic copper accumulation, especially in the liver, brain, and cornea.

Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumu.normalized_text: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), including pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumu.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterized by abnormal iron deposition in the basal ganglia, usually causing dystonia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline, or other movement disorders.

Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration due.normalized_text: Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration due to chronic liver disease or portosystemic shunting
Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration due.description: A neurologic complication of advanced chronic liver disease in which manganese and other metabolic toxins accumulate in the brain, often producing bilateral globus pallidus or basal ganglia T1 hyperintensity.

Cellulitis.description: A bacterial infection of the deeper skin and subcutaneous tissues, usually causing a warm, tender, expanding red area.

Arthropod bite reaction (including mosqu.normalized_text: Arthropod bite reaction (including mosquito, flea, bedbug, or other insect bite hypersensitivity)
Arthropod bite reaction (including mosqu.description: A localized inflammatory or allergic skin reaction following an arthropod bite, often producing itchy red papules, plaques, or swollen areas.

Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.normalized_text: Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis
Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.description: An expanding skin lesion caused by Borrelia infection after a tick bite; it may appear as a red expanding patch and is not always a classic bull's-eye rash.

Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.description: An inflammatory skin disorder characterized by tender red-to-violaceous papules, nodules, or plaques, frequently on the upper limbs, sometimes with fever or elevated inflammatory markers.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory reaction of subcutaneous fat causing tender red or bruise-like nodules, classically on the shins but occasionally at other sites.

Eagle syndrome.description: A symptomatic elongated styloid process or ossified stylohyoid ligament that can irritate nearby throat, cranial nerve, or vascular structures.

Ossification/calcification of the styloh.description: Mineralization of the ligament between the styloid process and hyoid bone; it may be an incidental imaging finding or may contribute to Eagle syndrome when symptomatic.

Elongated styloid process.description: An anatomical variant in which the temporal bone styloid process is longer than usual; it is often asymptomatic but can be associated with Eagle syndrome.

Insulinoma.description: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin inappropriately, causing fasting or recurrent hypoglycemia with elevated endogenous insulin and C-peptide levels.

Sulfonylurea or meglitinide-induced hypo.description: Hypoglycemia caused by insulin-secretagogue medications, which stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion and produce high insulin and C-peptide levels similar to insulinoma.

Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglyce.description: A condition involving diffuse pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction, resulting in excessive endogenous insulin release and recurrent hypoglycemia; it may occur after bariatric surgery or without a clear cause.

Insulin autoimmune syndrome (Hirata dise.description: A rare autoimmune disorder in which insulin autoantibodies bind insulin and can cause episodes of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia without exogenous insulin administration.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: A painful hypermobility of the false ribs, usually the 8th to 10th ribs, caused by laxity or disruption of interchondral attachments. Dynamic ultrasound may show abnormal movement or overriding of a rib over an adjacent rib.

Healed or healing rib fracture with call.normalized_text: Healed or healing rib fracture with callus formation
Healed or healing rib fracture with call.description: A prior rib fracture may heal with bony callus, cortical irregularity, thickening, or angulation that can create an abnormal contour on ultrasound.

Congenital rib deformity or rib fusion.normalized_text: Congenital rib deformity or rib fusion
Congenital rib deformity or rib fusion.description: A congenital chest-wall variation can produce an abnormal rib shape, partial fusion, bifid rib, or atypical spacing between adjacent ribs. These findings may be incidental or associated with chest-wall asymmetry.

Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis.description: A benign or secondary condition in which multiple gas-filled cysts develop within the bowel wall, usually in the submucosa or subserosa. It can appear as polypoid lesions at colonoscopy and as clustered radiolucent cysts on contrast imaging.

Colonic lymphangiomatosis.description: A rare benign malformation characterized by dilated lymphatic channels in the bowel wall, producing multiple submucosal cystic lesions that may resemble pneumatosis.

Colitis cystica profunda.description: A benign disorder in which mucin-filled cystically dilated colonic glands extend into the submucosa, often associated with chronic inflammation, rectal prolapse, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent eosinophilia, abnormal immature/dysplastic eosinophils, and evidence of a myeloid malignancy when defining PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2 rearrangements are absent.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase gene rearrangement
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms associated with eosinophilia and rearrangements involving genes such as PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2. These disorders may resemble chronic eosinophilic leukemia and can show myeloid dysplasia and anemia.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A syndrome of persistent, otherwise unexplained eosinophilia that can cause inflammatory organ injury, particularly involving the lungs, heart, skin, nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract. It is diagnosed after exclusion of secondary causes and clonal eosinophilic neoplasms.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: An eosinophil-rich necrotizing vasculitis that typically occurs in patients with asthma, allergic rhinosinusitis, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, and systemic inflammation. ANCA may be negative in many affected patients.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymph.description: A CD30-positive T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, often occurring in children and adolescents, that can involve lymph nodes and extranodal sites such as bowel, skin, bone, lung, and kidneys. The histology and immunostaining pattern shown are highly suggestive of this diagnosis.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells, usually CD30-positive, that commonly presents with lymphadenopathy and may spread to mediastinal and abdominal lymph nodes.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that frequently affects children and often presents with rapidly growing abdominal disease, bowel involvement, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and possible renal infiltration.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Acute malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, which can produce high parasitemia, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, hepatic dysfunction, and acute kidney injury. The rapid malaria test and blood smear showing multiple delicate ring forms, including peripheral/appliqué forms, strongly support this diagnosis.

Uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum mala.description: Malaria due to P. falciparum without definite evidence of life-threatening organ dysfunction. However, this patient has laboratory findings concerning for severe rather than uncomplicated disease.

Plasmodium vivax malaria.description: Malaria caused by P. vivax, typically associated with enlarged red cells, trophozoites, Schüffner stippling, thrombocytopenia, and possible splenomegaly. It is less consistent with the rapid-test and smear morphology shown.

Babesiosis.description: A tick-borne intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that can resemble malaria on blood smear and may cause hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, jaundice, liver enzyme elevation, and renal injury. The malaria rapid test and parasite morphology favor malaria instead.

Esophageal perforation with mediastinal.description: A full-thickness defect in the esophageal wall allowing saliva, food material, contrast, or infected fluid to enter the mediastinum; this is a medical emergency.

Acute mediastinitis.description: Severe infection and inflammation of the mediastinal tissues, commonly caused by esophageal perforation and leakage of contaminated esophageal contents.

Esophagomediastinal fistula.description: An abnormal tract or persistent opening between the esophagus and mediastinum, often developing after esophageal injury, surgery, infection, or perforation.

Intrathoracic extramedullary hematopoies.description: Compensatory production of blood cells outside the bone marrow, often forming bilateral paravertebral or pleural-based thoracic masses in chronic hemolytic anemia or myeloproliferative disease.

Primary myelofibrosis with extramedullar.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm in which bone-marrow fibrosis leads to blood formation in the spleen, liver, and sometimes thorax, causing massive splenomegaly and paravertebral masses.

Beta-thalassemia intermedia or another c.normalized_text: Beta-thalassemia intermedia or another chronic hemolytic anemia with extramedullary hematopoiesis
Beta-thalassemia intermedia or another c.description: Chronic ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis can cause marked splenic enlargement and paravertebral extramedullary hematopoietic masses, including in the thorax.

Lymphoma with mediastinal and splenic in.normalized_text: Lymphoma with mediastinal and splenic involvement
Lymphoma with mediastinal and splenic in.description: Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma can produce mediastinal/paravertebral lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, pleural effusions, and lung compression.

Hepatic encephalopathy.description: A reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by liver dysfunction and accumulation of neurotoxins such as ammonia. EEG commonly shows generalized slowing and high-amplitude triphasic waves.

Uremic encephalopathy.description: Diffuse brain dysfunction caused by severe renal failure and retention of uremic toxins. EEG may show generalized slowing and triphasic waves similar to those seen in hepatic encephalopathy.

Septic or toxic-metabolic encephalopathy.description: Global cerebral dysfunction caused by systemic infection, inflammation, hypoxia, electrolyte abnormalities, medications, or other metabolic disturbances. Generalized slowing and triphasic waves are common EEG findings.

Nonconvulsive status epilepticus.description: Persistent seizure activity without prominent convulsions, often presenting as confusion or reduced responsiveness. Periodic generalized discharges can resemble triphasic waves, although epileptic discharges more often show evolution in frequency, location, or morphology.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.description: A rapidly progressive prion neurodegenerative disease that can produce periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, typically in the context of rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and neurological decline.

Obturator hernia with small-bowel obstru.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal, often becoming incarcerated and causing mechanical small-bowel obstruction.

Femoral hernia with bowel obstruction.description: A hernia through the femoral canal that may trap small bowel and produce intestinal obstruction; it can resemble an obturator hernia on pelvic imaging.

Incarcerated inguinal hernia.description: Protrusion of bowel through the inguinal canal that becomes trapped, potentially leading to small-bowel obstruction and bowel ischemia.

Adhesive small-bowel obstruction.description: Mechanical obstruction of the small intestine caused by fibrous adhesions, most often after prior abdominal or pelvic surgery.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune microangiopathy affecting small vessels of the brain, retina, and inner ear. The classic triad is branch retinal artery occlusion, sensorineural hearing loss, and encephalopathy/characteristic corpus callosum lesions.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause white-matter and corpus callosum lesions, visual symptoms, and occasionally auditory pathway symptoms.

Branch retinal artery occlusion due to e.normalized_text: Branch retinal artery occlusion due to embolic or inflammatory retinal vasculopathy
Branch retinal artery occlusion due to e.description: Occlusion of a branch retinal artery causes focal retinal ischemia and corresponding visual-field loss. Causes include emboli, vascular risk factors, vasculitis, hypercoagulable states, and autoimmune disease.

Desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy (de.description: An inherited myofibrillar myopathy caused by DES variants, characterized by progressive skeletal-muscle weakness, abnormal desmin-positive protein aggregates in muscle, and sometimes cardiomyopathy or cardiac conduction disease.

Myofibrillar myopathy due to filamin-C m.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy due to filamin-C mutation (FLNC-related myofibrillar myopathy)
Myofibrillar myopathy due to filamin-C m.description: A dominantly inherited protein-aggregate myopathy caused by FLNC variants. It may cause adult-onset axial, proximal, distal, or respiratory muscle weakness, elevated CK, and protein inclusions on muscle biopsy.

Myotilin-related myofibrillar myopathy (.description: An autosomal-dominant myofibrillar myopathy caused by MYOT variants, usually presenting in adulthood with progressive limb, axial, or distal weakness and myofibrillar disorganization with protein inclusions on muscle biopsy.

Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy/myofibril.normalized_text: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy/myofibrillar myopathy due to Z-disc protein dysfunction, including BAG3- or CRYAB-related disease
Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy/myofibril.description: Inherited disorders affecting Z-disc and protein-quality-control pathways can produce progressive myopathy, elevated CK, and abnormal cytoplasmic protein aggregates. Some forms have multisystem manifestations.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: An aggressive mature B-cell neoplasm that may present with extensive bone-marrow and peripheral-blood involvement (Burkitt leukemia). It is characteristically associated with MYC rearrangement, most often t(8;14), and tumor cells may have deeply basophilic, vacuolated cytoplasm.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements
High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and.description: A highly aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma, historically termed double-hit or triple-hit lymphoma when MYC is rearranged together with BCL2 and/or BCL6. It can involve lymph nodes, extranodal sites, bone marrow, and blood and often has complex cytogenetic abnormalities.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A precursor B-cell malignancy characterized by proliferation of lymphoblasts in bone marrow and blood. Diagnosis requires immunophenotyping showing precursor markers such as TdT and usually CD34, rather than mature B-cell lymphoma markers alone.

Acute myeloid leukemia.description: A clonal myeloid malignancy with accumulation of myeloid blasts in marrow and often blood. Subclassification depends on morphology, flow cytometry, cytochemistry, and molecular/cytogenetic testing.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites, endemic in Mediterranean countries including Spain, typically involving the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

Hepatosplenic bartonellosis (cat-scratch.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic bartonellosis (cat-scratch disease with hepatic involvement)
Hepatosplenic bartonellosis (cat-scratch.description: Disseminated Bartonella henselae infection can cause multiple hepatic and splenic granulomas or microabscesses, often seen as hypoechoic lesions on ultrasound and hypodense lesions on CT.

Hepatic and splenic tuberculosis.description: Disseminated or extrapulmonary tuberculosis can produce multiple small granulomatous lesions in the liver and spleen, with hepatosplenomegaly.

Hepatic lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can infiltrate the liver and spleen diffusely or form multiple low-attenuation liver lesions, frequently accompanied by splenomegaly.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute proximal left anterior descending.normalized_text: Acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion with de Winter ECG pattern
Acute proximal left anterior descending.description: A de Winter pattern is an anterior STEMI equivalent, usually indicating acute proximal LAD occlusion. It features upsloping ST-segment depression at the J point in the anterior precordial leads with tall, symmetric hyperacute T waves, often with slight ST elevation in aVR.

Acute anterior myocardial infarction (hy.normalized_text: Acute anterior myocardial infarction (hyperacute/early LAD-territory infarction)
Acute anterior myocardial infarction (hy.description: An acute anterior myocardial infarction is myocardial injury from acute coronary obstruction affecting the LAD distribution. In very early stages, prominent broad-based hyperacute T waves may appear before conventional ST-segment elevation develops.

Hyperkalemia.description: Hyperkalemia is an elevated blood potassium level that can cause tall peaked T waves and, when severe, PR prolongation, P-wave flattening, QRS widening, and dangerous arrhythmias.

Congenital lobar emphysema.description: A congenital overinflation of one or more pulmonary lobes due to partial bronchial obstruction or abnormal airway cartilage, often presenting in neonates with progressive unilateral hyperlucency and mediastinal shift.

Bronchial atresia.description: A congenital interruption or obliteration of a bronchus that causes distal mucus impaction and hyperinflation of the affected lung segment through collateral ventilation.

Pulmonary sequestration, possibly a hybr.normalized_text: Pulmonary sequestration, possibly a hybrid congenital lung lesion
Pulmonary sequestration, possibly a hybr.description: Nonfunctioning congenital lung tissue without normal bronchial communication, usually supplied by an aberrant systemic artery from the descending thoracic or abdominal aorta. It may coexist with congenital pulmonary airway malformation.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A developmental malformation of the lower respiratory tract characterized by cystic or overexpanded abnormal lung tissue; some lesions have an associated systemic arterial supply and are termed hybrid CPAM-sequestration lesions.

Malignant hypertension with hyperplastic.description: Severe, rapidly progressive hypertension can cause concentric intimal thickening of small arteries and arterioles ('onion-skin' hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis), resulting in marked luminal narrowing.

Systemic sclerosis with scleroderma rena.normalized_text: Systemic sclerosis with scleroderma renal crisis
Systemic sclerosis with scleroderma rena.description: Systemic sclerosis may produce severe renal vascular injury with concentric intimal proliferation, narrowed arterioles, ischemia, and abrupt severe hypertension.

Thrombotic microangiopathy.description: A group of disorders characterized by endothelial injury, platelet-rich microthrombi, vascular narrowing, and sometimes onion-skin intimal changes; causes include thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic uremic syndrome, malignant hypertension, and autoimmune disease.

Basilar invagination.description: A craniovertebral junction abnormality in which the upper cervical spine, especially the odontoid process, migrates upward toward the skull base and may compress the brainstem or upper spinal cord.

Chiari I malformation.description: A condition in which the cerebellar tonsils descend through the foramen magnum, potentially obstructing cerebrospinal fluid flow and causing compression at the craniovertebral junction.

Atlantoaxial instability or atlantoaxial.description: Excessive movement or misalignment between the first and second cervical vertebrae that can cause instability and compression of the upper cervical spinal cord or brainstem.

Os odontoideum.description: A structural abnormality in which the odontoid process is separated from the body of the axis, often causing atlantoaxial instability and possible cervicomedullary compression.

Lactobacillus-associated infective endoc.description: Infective endocarditis caused by Lactobacillus species, uncommon Gram-positive organisms that are often intrinsically highly resistant to vancomycin and may show resistance to cephalosporins. It can produce large destructive valvular vegetations and regurgitation.

Enterococcal infective endocarditis due.normalized_text: Enterococcal infective endocarditis due to vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus
Enterococcal infective endocarditis due.description: Endocarditis caused by Enterococcus species, including vancomycin-resistant strains. Enterococci can cause persistent bloodstream infection, valve destruction, vegetations, and valvular insufficiency.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infective e.description: A rare bacterial endocarditis caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive rod often associated with animal or fish exposure. It is characteristically resistant to vancomycin and may cause severe destructive native-valve infection.

Acute pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of a pulmonary artery by thrombus, usually originating from deep veins in the legs or pelvis. The CT image shows a contrast-filling defect in a left pulmonary arterial branch, which is characteristic of pulmonary embolism.

Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease.description: Persistent organized thrombus in the pulmonary arteries after prior embolic events; it can lead to chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

Pulmonary artery sarcoma.description: A rare malignant tumor arising from the pulmonary artery that can resemble pulmonary embolism by producing an intraluminal filling defect.

Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis.description: An acute viral encephalitis caused most often by HSV-1, characteristically involving the medial temporal lobes, insulae, and inferior frontal regions.

Autoimmune limbic encephalitis.description: Inflammation of the limbic system due to neuronal autoantibodies, such as anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B receptor, AMPA receptor, or paraneoplastic antibodies.

Human herpesvirus-6 encephalitis.description: A viral encephalitis most often seen in immunocompromised patients, particularly following hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, with preferential involvement of the mesial temporal lobes.

Neurosyphilis with meningovascular or en.normalized_text: Neurosyphilis with meningovascular or encephalitic involvement
Neurosyphilis with meningovascular or en.description: Central nervous system infection with Treponema pallidum that can cause meningitis, vascular inflammation, cognitive symptoms, and occasionally focal parenchymal abnormalities.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: Severe atypical pneumonia caused by Legionella species, often associated with hyponatremia, elevated liver enzymes, rhabdomyolysis, and respiratory failure.

Severe community-acquired bacterial pneu.normalized_text: Severe community-acquired bacterial pneumonia with sepsis
Severe community-acquired bacterial pneu.description: Severe bacterial infection of the lungs causing systemic inflammation, sepsis, organ dysfunction, and acute respiratory failure.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.normalized_text: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) or macrophage activation syndrome
Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by excessive immune activation, often triggered by severe infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease.

Severe COVID-19 pneumonia.description: Severe SARS-CoV-2 infection can produce viral pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, hyperinflammation, myocardial injury, and elevated ferritin and liver enzymes.

Influenza-associated viral pneumonia wit.description: Severe influenza can cause viral pneumonia, acute respiratory failure, muscle injury/rhabdomyolysis, transaminitis, and occasionally cardiac injury.

Tumor-induced osteomalacia due to a phos.normalized_text: Tumor-induced osteomalacia due to a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor
Tumor-induced osteomalacia due to a phos.description: A rare acquired paraneoplastic disorder caused by a usually small mesenchymal tumor that secretes excess FGF23, producing renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemia, impaired bone mineralization, and osteomalacia. Surgical removal typically normalizes phosphate and FGF23 rapidly.

FGF23-secreting mesenchymal neoplasm oth.normalized_text: FGF23-secreting mesenchymal neoplasm other than classic phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor
FGF23-secreting mesenchymal neoplasm oth.description: Rare tumors such as hemangiopericytoma/solitary fibrous tumor, giant-cell tumor, or other mesenchymal neoplasms can occasionally produce FGF23 and cause oncogenic osteomalacia.

X-linked hypophosphatemia.description: An inherited disorder, usually due to PHEX mutations, in which excess FGF23 causes chronic renal phosphate wasting and defective bone mineralization.

Autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rick.description: A hereditary FGF23-mediated phosphate-wasting disorder caused by variants that reduce degradation of FGF23, leading to hypophosphatemia and osteomalacia or rickets.

Disseminated cystic echinococcosis (hyda.normalized_text: Disseminated cystic echinococcosis (hydatid disease due to Echinococcus granulosus)
Disseminated cystic echinococcosis (hyda.description: A parasitic infection in which hydatid cysts develop in organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, and heart. Spain is an endemic region, and the images suggest cystic lesions involving the brain, heart, and liver.

Cerebral hydatid cyst.description: A rare manifestation of cystic echinococcosis in which a slowly enlarging fluid-filled parasitic cyst develops in the brain, potentially causing neurologic deficits or raised intracranial pressure.

Cardiac hydatid cyst.description: Hydatid disease involving the myocardium or cardiac chambers. It is uncommon but may cause arrhythmia, obstruction, embolic events, or rupture depending on cyst location.

Hepatic hydatid cyst.description: The most common form of cystic echinococcosis, characterized by one or more parasitic cysts in the liver. It may be asymptomatic or cause abdominal discomfort, biliary complications, or infection.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A rare autosomal-recessive ciliopathy, commonly caused by variants in genes such as WDR35, IFT122, IFT43, IFT52, or WDR60. It combines craniosynostosis/dolichocephaly, ectodermal abnormalities, short-rib skeletal dysplasia, and progressive kidney disease.

Short-rib thoracic dysplasia / Jeune syn.description: A group of skeletal ciliopathies characterized by short ribs, a narrow thorax, variable limb shortening, renal disease, and sometimes retinal or other ocular abnormalities. Several genes overlap biologically with cranioectodermal dysplasia.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: A renal-skeletal ciliopathy usually involving cone-rod retinal dystrophy, chronic kidney disease or nephronophthisis, and skeletal abnormalities such as cone-shaped epiphyses and phalangeal shortening.

Ellis-van Creveld syndrome.description: An autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia with short limbs, short ribs, narrow thorax, nail and tooth abnormalities, and characteristic hand and foot findings; congenital heart disease is common.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disease of skin and muscle. Characteristic skin findings include violaceous, scaly papules over the knuckles (Gottron papules) and erythema over extensor joints; muscle weakness may or may not be present initially.

Psoriasis.description: A chronic immune-mediated skin disease causing well-demarcated erythematous plaques with scale. It can involve the hands, fingers, nails, and extensor surfaces.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that commonly affects intrathoracic lymph nodes and may cause a variety of skin lesions, including papules, plaques, and nodules.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (bilateral Pe.description: Childhood avascular necrosis of the femoral head epiphysis, causing fragmentation, flattening, deformity of the femoral head, and possible early hip osteoarthritis. It can occasionally affect both hips.

Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.description: A hereditary skeletal dysplasia characterized by abnormal development of multiple joint epiphyses, particularly the hips and knees, leading to irregular femoral heads and premature osteoarthritis.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip with.normalized_text: Developmental dysplasia of the hip with secondary osteoarthritis
Developmental dysplasia of the hip with.description: Abnormal development of the acetabulum and/or femoral head that may cause hip instability, subluxation, altered femoral-head shape, and premature degenerative arthritis.

Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia.description: A group of inherited skeletal dysplasias affecting the spine and joint epiphyses, often causing bilateral hip dysplasia, flattened femoral heads, restricted mobility, and early osteoarthritis.

Infected hepatic hydatid cyst (echinococ.normalized_text: Infected hepatic hydatid cyst (echinococcal liver cyst with intralesional gas)
Infected hepatic hydatid cyst (echinococ.description: A hydatid cyst is a parasitic cyst caused by Echinococcus species, often involving the liver. Infection, communication with the biliary tree, or rupture can introduce gas into the cyst, producing an air-fluid level.

Pyogenic liver abscess with gas formatio.normalized_text: Pyogenic liver abscess with gas formation
Pyogenic liver abscess with gas formatio.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a bacterial collection of pus in the liver. Gas-forming organisms can produce intralesional gas and an air-fluid level, particularly in large abscesses.

Infected simple hepatic cyst.description: A simple hepatic cyst is a benign fluid-filled liver lesion that can rarely become infected or communicate with the biliary tract, resulting in internal gas and an air-fluid level.

Pneumoperitoneum from hollow-viscus perf.description: Pneumoperitoneum is free gas in the peritoneal cavity, most commonly due to perforation of the stomach, duodenum, or bowel. It may be visible beneath the diaphragm on an upright chest radiograph.

Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infecti.description: A congenital viral infection that can cause abnormal brain development, periventricular injury, white-matter disease, ventriculomegaly, cortical malformations, and characteristic anterior temporal lobe cysts.

Congenital toxoplasmosis.description: A fetal infection caused by Toxoplasma gondii that may produce hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcifications, seizures, chorioretinitis, and developmental impairment.

Periventricular leukomalacia due to pren.normalized_text: Periventricular leukomalacia due to prenatal or perinatal hypoxic-ischemic injury
Periventricular leukomalacia due to pren.description: White-matter injury around the lateral ventricles, usually related to fetal or premature neonatal hypoxia-ischemia; it can result in volume loss, ventricular enlargement, motor impairment, and developmental delay.

Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome.description: A genetic inflammatory encephalopathy that can mimic congenital viral infection and may cause white-matter abnormalities, cerebral atrophy, intracranial calcifications, developmental delay, and neurologic dysfunction.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the j.normalized_text: Primary hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the jejunum
Primary hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the j.description: A rare extrahepatic adenocarcinoma with morphologic and immunophenotypic differentiation resembling hepatocellular carcinoma; it may produce AFP and express hepatocytic markers such as glypican-3.

Jejunal adenocarcinoma, poorly different.description: A primary malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine, usually presenting as an obstructing or ulcerated intestinal mass. Most intestinal-type tumors express CDX2 and often CK20/SATB2, although poorly differentiated tumors can lose these markers.

Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma invo.normalized_text: Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma involving the jejunum
Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma invo.description: Hepatocellular carcinoma can rarely metastasize to the gastrointestinal tract and may show AFP and glypican-3 expression with a hepatoid morphology.

Extragonadal yolk sac tumor involving th.normalized_text: Extragonadal yolk sac tumor involving the small bowel
Extragonadal yolk sac tumor involving th.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor that can produce AFP and may express SALL4 and glypican-3. Primary gastrointestinal involvement is very rare and should be distinguished from hepatoid adenocarcinoma.

Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.normalized_text: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting ectopic gastric mucosa. Acid-related ulceration of adjacent ileal mucosa can cause substantial gastrointestinal bleeding. The serial nuclear images are compatible with focal tracer uptake from ectopic gastric mucosa, a typical finding on technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy for Meckel diverticulum.

Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.normalized_text: Enteric duplication cyst containing ectopic gastric mucosa
Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.description: An intestinal duplication cyst is a rare congenital malformation that can contain ectopic gastric mucosa. It may demonstrate technetium-99m pertechnetate uptake similar to a Meckel diverticulum and can bleed because of acid-induced ulceration of adjacent bowel.

Bleeding peptic ulcer disease.description: Gastric or duodenal ulceration can cause acute or chronic upper gastrointestinal bleeding, resulting in severe iron-deficiency anemia and an increased reticulocyte response after blood loss.

Small-bowel angiodysplasia with gastroin.description: Angiodysplasia consists of fragile dilated intestinal blood vessels, often in the small bowel or colon, that can cause intermittent occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (P.description: Abnormal direct connections between pulmonary arteries and veins, producing enhancing rounded vascular lesions with feeding and draining vessels on CT. They may be solitary or multiple.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.normalized_text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An inherited vascular dysplasia characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, commonly involving the lungs, nose, gastrointestinal tract, liver, and brain. Multiple PAVMs strongly suggest this condition.

Pulmonary artery aneurysms or pseudoaneu.description: Focal dilatations of branches of the pulmonary artery that can appear as strongly enhancing rounded vascular opacities. They may occur with vasculitis, infection, trauma, pulmonary hypertension, or congenital vascular disease.

Post-primary pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection that commonly affects the upper lobes and may cause progressive consolidation, cavitation, fibrosis, and traction bronchiectasis.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary d.description: Chronic pulmonary infection caused by environmental mycobacteria, such as Mycobacterium avium complex or Mycobacterium kansasii, which can produce fibrocavitary upper-lobe disease and bronchiectasis.

Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis.description: A chronic Aspergillus lung infection occurring in previously damaged lungs, characterized by one or more progressive cavities, adjacent pleural or parenchymal thickening, and sometimes fungal balls within cavities.

Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with pos.normalized_text: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with postinfectious bronchiectasis
Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with pos.description: Severe bacterial pneumonia can cause lung necrosis, cavitation, abscess formation, and residual localized bronchiectasis; pathogens may include Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or anaerobic bacteria.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A severe demyelinating central nervous system infection caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus, most often occurring during immunosuppression, including natalizumab treatment.

Natalizumab-associated JC virus central.normalized_text: Natalizumab-associated JC virus central nervous system infection
Natalizumab-associated JC virus central.description: JC virus reactivation involving the central nervous system in a patient receiving natalizumab; the most clinically important manifestation is PML, but other JCV neurologic syndromes can occur.

JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV.normalized_text: JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV GCN)
JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV.description: A rare JC virus infection affecting cerebellar granule neurons, typically causing progressive cerebellar dysfunction in immunosuppressed patients and sometimes occurring with natalizumab therapy.

Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) w.normalized_text: Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) with cardiac involvement
Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) w.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in multiple tissues. Cardiac involvement commonly causes concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, conduction abnormalities, and characteristic lamellar inclusions on electron microscopy.

Sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disorder characterized by unexplained left-ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetric, which can cause abnormal ECG findings, diastolic dysfunction, arrhythmias, and obstruction of the left-ventricular outflow tract.

Drug-induced phospholipidosis, particula.normalized_text: Drug-induced phospholipidosis, particularly hydroxychloroquine- or chloroquine-associated cardiomyopathy
Drug-induced phospholipidosis, particula.description: Long-term exposure to hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine can cause lysosomal phospholipid accumulation in cardiac muscle, producing ventricular hypertrophy, conduction abnormalities, and lamellar inclusions that can resemble Fabry disease.

Hydronephrosis.description: Dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces caused by impaired urine drainage, often from urinary tract obstruction. The ultrasound appearance is suggestive of a dilated collecting system.

Ureteropelvic junction obstruction.description: A blockage at the junction between the renal pelvis and ureter that can produce hydronephrosis, sometimes without ureteral dilation. It may be congenital or acquired.

Obstructing ureteral stone (ureterolithi.description: A urinary stone lodged in the ureter can obstruct urine flow and cause upstream hydronephrosis. Stones may not always be directly visible on a single ultrasound image.

Pyonephrosis.description: Infection of an obstructed renal collecting system, usually occurring when hydronephrosis is complicated by bacterial infection. Ultrasound can show collecting-system dilation with internal debris.

Lepromatous leprosy (multibacillary Hans.description: A disseminated form of infection with Mycobacterium leprae, characterized by numerous symmetric skin papules, nodules, plaques, and diffuse facial infiltration; the ears and face are commonly involved.

Histoid leprosy.description: A nodular variant of multibacillary leprosy with firm, dome-shaped, skin-colored to reddish-brown papules and nodules containing large numbers of leprosy bacilli.

Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.description: A rare disseminated form of Leishmania infection causing widespread nonulcerated papules, plaques, and nodules, often in people with impaired cellular immune responses.

Cutaneous cryptococcosis.description: A fungal infection, usually in immunocompromised individuals, that may cause umbilicated papules, acne-like lesions, nodules, ulcers, or cellulitis-like skin lesions.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis (lupus pernio or n.normalized_text: Cutaneous sarcoidosis (lupus pernio or nodular sarcoidosis)
Cutaneous sarcoidosis (lupus pernio or n.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that can produce papules, plaques, and nodules on the face, especially involving the nose, cheeks, and ears.

Renal hydatid cyst (renal echinococcosis.description: A parasitic cyst caused by Echinococcus granulosus. Renal involvement is uncommon but can occur in endemic Mediterranean regions, including Spain. Imaging may show a large complex cyst with internal daughter cysts or septated cystic components.

Cystic renal cell carcinoma.description: A malignant kidney tumor that may appear partly or predominantly cystic, often with thick walls, septations, nodules, or enhancement on contrast CT.

Renal abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in or around the kidney, usually due to ascending urinary infection or bloodstream spread. It can appear as a complex cystic renal lesion with internal debris or septations.

Complex renal cyst (Bosniak IIF-III cyst.description: A renal cyst with septa, wall thickening, calcification, or more complex internal features. Some complex cysts are benign, while others require surveillance or surgery because of possible malignancy.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with pu.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with pu.description: A rapidly progressive zoonotic bloodstream infection caused by a fusiform gram-negative rod, usually transmitted through dog or cat bites, scratches, or saliva exposure. It can cause overwhelming sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, multiorgan failure, and extensive purpura.

Septic shock with disseminated intravasc.normalized_text: Septic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Septic shock with disseminated intravasc.description: A severe systemic response to infection causing circulatory failure and widespread activation of coagulation. Consumption of platelets and clotting factors produces bleeding, purpura, schistocytes, organ ischemia, and multiorgan dysfunction.

Meningococcal septicemia with purpura fu.description: Invasive Neisseria meningitidis infection can rapidly cause sepsis, thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemorrhagic purpura, shock, and multiorgan failure.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy, usually caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with possible kidney, neurologic, and fever-related manifestations.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

Left atrial myxoma with cardioembolic is.normalized_text: Left atrial myxoma with cardioembolic ischemic stroke
Left atrial myxoma with cardioembolic is.description: A left atrial myxoma is a benign primary cardiac tumor that can shed emboli into the systemic circulation, causing acute cerebral arterial occlusion and ischemic stroke.

Cardioembolic stroke due to infective en.normalized_text: Cardioembolic stroke due to infective endocarditis with valvular vegetation
Cardioembolic stroke due to infective en.description: Infective endocarditis is infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve. Friable vegetations may embolize and cause cerebral infarction or arterial occlusion.

Left-sided intracardiac thrombus causing.normalized_text: Left-sided intracardiac thrombus causing cardioembolic stroke
Left-sided intracardiac thrombus causing.description: A thrombus in the left atrium, left atrial appendage, left ventricle, or on a cardiac valve can embolize through the arterial circulation and obstruct a cerebral artery.

Cardiac papillary fibroelastoma with cer.normalized_text: Cardiac papillary fibroelastoma with cerebral embolism
Cardiac papillary fibroelastoma with cer.description: Papillary fibroelastoma is a small benign valvular cardiac tumor, often involving the aortic or mitral valve. It may cause stroke through embolization of tumor fragments or associated thrombus.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.description: An invasive gland-forming cancer arising from pancreatic ducts, commonly located in the pancreatic head and causing obstruction of the distal common bile duct. Imaging and histology are consistent with an infiltrative pancreatic-region adenocarcinoma with desmoplastic stroma and probable liver metastases.

Distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A bile-duct adenocarcinoma arising in the distal common bile duct. It produces painless obstructive jaundice and can be difficult to distinguish from pancreatic-head adenocarcinoma because both may cause distal biliary obstruction and have similar gland-forming histology.

Ampullary adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the ampulla of Vater, where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct empty into the duodenum. It can cause biliary obstruction and may resemble pancreatic-head cancer or distal cholangiocarcinoma on imaging and biopsy.

Crohn disease (terminal ileitis).description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that commonly involves the terminal ileum and ileocecal region, causing bowel-wall inflammation, thickening, narrowing, and possible fistulas or strictures.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis involving the gastrointestinal tract, most often affecting the ileocecal region and potentially causing mural thickening, inflammatory masses, strictures, obstruction, and regional lymph-node enlargement.

Yersinia enterocolitica ileitis.description: A bacterial intestinal infection that can inflame the terminal ileum, cecum, and mesenteric lymph nodes, sometimes mimicking appendicitis or Crohn disease.

Ileocecal intussusception.description: A condition in which a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, often involving terminal ileum and colon; in adults it may occur because of a lead point such as a polyp, tumor, or inflammatory lesion.

Ileocecal neoplasm (such as adenocarcino.normalized_text: Ileocecal neoplasm (such as adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, or neuroendocrine tumor)
Ileocecal neoplasm (such as adenocarcino.description: A tumor involving the terminal ileum, cecum, or ileocecal valve that may produce focal bowel-wall thickening, a mass, obstruction, or intussusception.

Nutritional rickets (vitamin D deficienc.description: A disorder of defective bone mineralization in growing children, commonly due to vitamin D deficiency, causing widened and irregular growth plates and metaphyseal cupping or fraying.

Infantile scurvy (vitamin C deficiency).description: Vitamin C deficiency causing impaired collagen formation, bone pain, bleeding, and characteristic dense metaphyseal lines, metaphyseal spurs, and subperiosteal hemorrhage on radiographs.

Growth-arrest (Harris) lines following p.normalized_text: Growth-arrest (Harris) lines following prior systemic illness or nutritional stress
Growth-arrest (Harris) lines following p.description: Transverse dense metaphyseal lines that can develop after temporary interruption and subsequent recovery of bone growth, such as after illness, malnutrition, or metabolic stress.

Keratosis pilaris.description: A common benign follicular keratinization disorder in which keratin plugs hair follicles, producing rough, small follicular papules.

Trichostasis spinulosa.description: A follicular disorder caused by retention of multiple fine vellus hairs and keratin within dilated follicular openings, producing dark plugs or spiny papules.

Disseminated and recurrent infundibulofo.description: An uncommon inflammatory follicular eruption characterized by widespread asymptomatic or mildly itchy follicular papules, often on the trunk and extremities, with lymphocytic inflammation around the follicular infundibulum.

Lichen spinulosus.description: A variant of follicular keratosis pilaris characterized by grouped follicular papules with central keratotic spines, often forming rough plaques.

Pityriasis folliculorum due to Demodex i.normalized_text: Pityriasis folliculorum due to Demodex infestation
Pityriasis folliculorum due to Demodex i.description: A follicular eruption associated with increased Demodex mites, typically causing follicular scaling, plugs, rough texture, and facial redness.

Cutaneous loxoscelism (dermonecrotic spi.normalized_text: Cutaneous loxoscelism (dermonecrotic spider bite, potentially Loxosceles rufescens)
Cutaneous loxoscelism (dermonecrotic spi.description: A local necrotic reaction after a bite from a recluse spider. Loxosceles rufescens occurs in Mediterranean regions including Spain and can cause painful inflammation, purpura, blistering, ulceration, and necrosis through vascular injury.

Livedoid vasculopathy.description: A thrombotic disorder of small skin vessels, usually affecting the lower legs and ankles. It causes painful recurrent purpuric lesions and shallow ulcers that heal with porcelain-white or stellate scars.

Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (leuko.description: Inflammation of small dermal blood vessels that commonly produces palpable purpura on the legs and can occasionally cause hemorrhagic blisters, necrosis, and ulceration.

Pyoderma gangrenosum.description: An inflammatory neutrophilic dermatosis that causes rapidly progressive painful ulcers with undermined violaceous borders, often associated with inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis, or hematologic disease.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis.description: A parasitic skin infection transmitted by sandflies and present in parts of Spain. It usually causes a chronic papule, nodule, or painless ulcer with raised borders.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Malignant melanoma (amelanotic or poorly.normalized_text: Malignant melanoma (amelanotic or poorly pigmented melanoma)
Malignant melanoma (amelanotic or poorly.description: An aggressive malignant tumor of melanocytic cells that may show epithelioid or spindle-cell morphology and immunohistochemical positivity for melanocytic markers such as S-100, SOX10, HMB-45, or Melan-A. Some melanomas contain little or no visible melanin.

Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue (malig.normalized_text: Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue (malignant melanoma of soft parts)
Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue (malig.description: A rare malignant soft-tissue tumor with melanocytic differentiation, often composed of nests or fascicles of spindle and epithelioid cells. It commonly expresses S-100, SOX10, HMB-45, and Melan-A and is typically associated with an EWSR1-ATF1 or EWSR1-CREB1 fusion.

Metastatic melanoma.description: Melanoma can spread to lymph nodes, skin, soft tissue, viscera, or other organs and may present histologically as a poorly pigmented malignant epithelioid-cell tumor with melanocytic-marker positivity.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A rare, usually low-grade pancreatic tumor characterized by solid and pseudopapillary areas, hemorrhagic/degenerative change, and relatively uniform polygonal tumor cells. It often forms a large well-circumscribed mass.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm derived from pancreatic neuroendocrine cells that may be nonfunctioning and present as a large pancreatic mass, or functioning and cause hormone-related symptoms.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: An uncommon malignant pancreatic epithelial tumor showing acinar differentiation. It can form a large, circumscribed solid mass with necrosis and hemorrhage.

Pancreatoblastoma.description: A rare malignant pancreatic tumor, predominantly occurring in children, with acinar differentiation and characteristic squamoid corpuscles. Adult cases are uncommon.

Darier disease (keratosis follicularis),.description: A genetic disorder of keratinization characterized by greasy, crusted, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques, often in seborrheic or flexural areas. Histology typically shows acantholytic dyskeratosis with corps ronds and grains.

Hailey-Hailey disease (benign familial p.description: An inherited acantholytic skin disorder causing recurrent painful erosions, fissures, crusted plaques, and maceration in intertriginous sites such as the axillae, groin, and neck.

Verrucous epidermal nevus.description: A benign cutaneous mosaic disorder producing persistent linear or localized hyperpigmented, rough, papillomatous, or verrucous plaques, usually beginning early in life.

Nevus comedonicus.description: A follicular hamartoma characterized by grouped dilated follicular openings filled with dark keratin plugs, resembling comedones; lesions may become inflamed or form verrucous plaques.

Conventional chondrosarcoma of the ilium.description: A malignant cartilage-producing bone tumor that commonly arises in the pelvis and may form a large expansile lytic bone lesion with characteristic chondroid matrix calcifications.

Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.description: A rare, aggressive subtype of chondrosarcoma composed of undifferentiated small cells and cartilage, often affecting the pelvis and producing a destructive mass with areas of calcification.

Pelvic osteosarcoma.description: A malignant primary bone tumor that produces osteoid matrix and can occur in the pelvis, causing destructive bone change, a large soft-tissue mass, and internal mineralization.

Classic anti-GAD stiff-person syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb stiffness, painful muscle spasms, and motor hyperexcitability; high-titer glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies are common.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe stiff-person-spectrum disorder with rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms, myoclonus, brainstem dysfunction, autonomic symptoms, and sometimes encephalopathy; it is often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies but may overlap with anti-GAD autoimmunity.

Anti-GAD cerebellar ataxia.description: An autoimmune cerebellar syndrome associated with high-titer GAD antibodies, typically causing gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus, and impaired coordination; it can coexist with other anti-GAD neurologic syndromes.

Neuromyotonia (Isaacs syndrome).description: A peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder causing muscle twitching, cramps, stiffness, myokymia, delayed muscle relaxation, and characteristic spontaneous repetitive discharges on EMG; it is often associated with CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies.

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) with scalp necrosis
Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis.description: A large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting cranial branches of the carotid artery, typically in older adults. Severe ischemia of scalp arteries can rarely cause painful ulcers or scalp necrosis.

Atherosclerotic carotid or subclavian ar.normalized_text: Atherosclerotic carotid or subclavian artery disease causing scalp ischemia
Atherosclerotic carotid or subclavian ar.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing or occlusion of major cervical arteries can reduce blood flow to the scalp, especially when collateral circulation is limited, and may lead to ischemic skin ulceration.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic inflammatory large-vessel vasculitis involving the aorta and its major branches. Stenosis of subclavian, carotid, or other arch vessels can produce ischemic manifestations.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause painful skin nodules, ulcers, livedo reticularis, peripheral neuropathy, and organ ischemia.

Visceral leishmaniasis (Mediterranean ka.normalized_text: Visceral leishmaniasis (Mediterranean kala-azar due to Leishmania infantum)
Visceral leishmaniasis (Mediterranean ka.description: A systemic protozoal infection caused in Spain most commonly by Leishmania infantum. Amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) can be seen within macrophages in bone marrow or other reticuloendothelial tissue, and marked polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia may occur.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species. Small intracellular yeasts may be found within macrophages and can resemble Leishmania amastigotes on microscopy, especially in bone marrow specimens.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis.description: A localized Leishmania infection that usually produces one or more chronic skin ulcers or nodules after sandfly exposure. Amastigotes are usually demonstrated from skin lesions rather than bone marrow.

Wells syndrome (eosinophilic cellulitis).description: An uncommon inflammatory skin disorder characterized by recurrent cellulitis-like red plaques, sometimes with central vesicles, bullae, crusting, or induration. Biopsy commonly shows dermal eosinophilic inflammation and collagen 'flame figures.'

Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.normalized_text: Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis
Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.description: An expanding erythematous skin lesion occurring after an Ixodes tick bite and representing early Lyme disease. It may become annular or develop central clearing, although atypical crusted lesions can occur at the bite site.

Arthropod bite reaction.description: A localized inflammatory or hypersensitivity reaction after a bite from a tick, mosquito, spider, flea, or other arthropod. It can cause redness, swelling, blistering, excoriation, and crusting.

Bacterial cellulitis or ecthyma.description: A bacterial skin infection, often caused by streptococci or staphylococci, that produces warm, tender expanding erythema. Ecthyma is a deeper crusted bacterial infection that can form a yellow-brown adherent crust.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B).description: A disorder of parathyroid hormone resistance caused by abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. The methylation pattern shown, with increased NESP methylation and loss of methylation at other GNAS differentially methylated regions, is characteristic of PHP1B.

Autosomal dominant pseudohypoparathyroid.description: A familial form of PHP1B, often due to maternal genetic or epigenetic defects affecting GNAS methylation, commonly involving STX16-related regulatory regions. It produces renal resistance to PTH without necessarily causing the skeletal features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A).description: A form of PTH resistance caused by maternally inherited inactivating mutations in GNAS. It is often associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy, including short stature, round face, obesity, brachydactyly, and possible resistance to other hormones.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 2.description: A rare form of PTH resistance in which the renal cyclic-AMP response to exogenous PTH is preserved but the phosphaturic response is impaired. It causes hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary elevation of PTH.

Chronic kidney disease with secondary hy.normalized_text: Chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Chronic kidney disease with secondary hy.description: Reduced kidney function causes phosphate retention, low calcitriol production, hypocalcemia, and compensatory elevation of PTH. It is a common cause of the biochemical combination of hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and high PTH.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, often causing reticuloendothelial involvement of the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lungs, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Tissue typically shows granulomatous inflammation with small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania species, endemic in parts of Spain, characterized by invasion of macrophages in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow and commonly causing pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and liver dysfunction.

Disseminated tuberculosis with hepatic a.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with hepatic and splenic involvement
Disseminated tuberculosis with hepatic a.description: Miliary or disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the liver, spleen, bone marrow, kidneys, and lungs, producing granulomas, cytopenias, cholestatic hepatitis, and systemic inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: Systemic infection with Cryptococcus species, usually in advanced cellular immunodeficiency, which can involve the lungs, bloodstream, central nervous system, liver, spleen, and kidneys. Organisms may be visible in tissue with special fungal stains.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.normalized_text: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by disseminated infection
Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infections such as histoplasmosis, leishmaniasis, tuberculosis, or viral infection. It can cause cytopenias, hepatitis, coagulopathy, renal injury, and marked LDH elevation.

Ovarian clear cell carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial ovarian tumor characterized by clear, glycogen-rich cells and often associated with endometriosis. It may present as a pelvic or ovarian mass.

Ovarian steroid cell tumor, not otherwis.normalized_text: Ovarian steroid cell tumor, not otherwise specified
Ovarian steroid cell tumor, not otherwis.description: A rare sex-cord stromal ovarian tumor composed of steroid-producing cells, frequently containing abundant eosinophilic or vacuolated cytoplasm. Some tumors produce androgens and can cause virilization.

Ovarian Leydig cell tumor.description: A usually small benign ovarian sex-cord stromal tumor composed of androgen-producing Leydig cells. It is often located near the ovarian hilum and may cause virilizing symptoms.

Syringomyelia.description: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, often in the cervical region. It may be congenital, idiopathic, familial, or secondary to impaired cerebrospinal-fluid flow.

Chiari I malformation-associated syringo.description: A syrinx caused by downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, which disrupts cerebrospinal-fluid circulation and can produce cervical syringomyelia.

Idiopathic or familial syringomyelia.description: Syringomyelia occurring without an identified Chiari malformation, tumor, trauma, infection, or other clear obstruction to cerebrospinal-fluid flow; rare familial cases have been reported.

Spinal cord ependymoma with associated s.normalized_text: Spinal cord ependymoma with associated syrinx
Spinal cord ependymoma with associated s.description: An intramedullary spinal cord tumor that can obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid flow and lead to formation of a syrinx above or below the tumor.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with he.normalized_text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with hemorrhagic venous infarcts
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with he.description: Thrombosis of a dural venous sinus, particularly the superior sagittal sinus, can cause bilateral parasagittal cortical edema, diffusion restriction, venous infarction, and petechial hemorrhage.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.normalized_text: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) with hemorrhagic or cytotoxic features
Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: PRES is a neurotoxic edema syndrome often associated with severe hypertension, renal disease, eclampsia, immunosuppressive drugs, or systemic inflammation. It commonly affects bilateral parieto-occipital regions and may occasionally show restricted diffusion or microhemorrhage.

Acute ischemic stroke involving bilatera.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke involving bilateral cortical territories
Acute ischemic stroke involving bilatera.description: Acute arterial cerebral infarction causes restricted diffusion due to cytotoxic edema. Multiple bilateral lesions can occur with embolic disease, hypoperfusion, or vasculitis.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related infl.normalized_text: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation or amyloid-related imaging abnormality
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related infl.description: Inflammation around amyloid-laden cortical vessels can produce asymmetric or bilateral cortical-subcortical edema and numerous lobar microbleeds, usually in older adults.

Intramedullary spinal cord sarcoidosis (.description: A granulomatous inflammatory manifestation of sarcoidosis involving the spinal cord, often producing an enhancing cervical intramedullary lesion and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy.

Spinal cord tuberculosis (intramedullary.normalized_text: Spinal cord tuberculosis (intramedullary tuberculoma or tuberculous myelitis)
Spinal cord tuberculosis (intramedullary.description: Tuberculosis can rarely involve the spinal cord, causing an intramedullary inflammatory mass or tuberculoma with granulomatous inflammation and giant cells.

Fungal granulomatous myelitis.description: Fungal infections such as histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, or other endemic fungi can rarely cause granulomatous inflammation involving the central nervous system and spinal cord.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A chronic bacterial infection caused by Actinomyces species that can produce mass-like consolidation, abscesses, cavitation, and suppurative granulomatous inflammation. It can mimic tuberculosis or lung cancer.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the lungs, often producing cavitary consolidation and granulomatous inflammation. Although classically upper-lobe predominant, lower-lobe disease can occur.

Bacterial lung abscess / necrotizing pne.description: A severe bacterial pulmonary infection causing necrosis of lung tissue, cavitation, air-fluid levels, and surrounding consolidation; aspiration-related infection commonly involves dependent lower lobes.

Pulmonary hydatid disease with secondary.normalized_text: Pulmonary hydatid disease with secondary infection or rupture
Pulmonary hydatid disease with secondary.description: Pulmonary infection by Echinococcus granulosus, which is endemic in parts of Spain. A hydatid cyst may become complicated by rupture or infection and can appear as a cavitary lesion with surrounding consolidation.

Acanthocephaliasis (infection with an ac.normalized_text: Acanthocephaliasis (infection with an acanthocephalan such as Macracanthorhynchus hirudinaceus)
Acanthocephaliasis (infection with an ac.description: A rare intestinal helminth infection caused by thorny-headed worms. These parasites have a thick body wall, muscular layers, and reproductive structures that can be seen in histologic sections. Human infection may follow ingestion of infected intermediate hosts or contaminated food.

Linguatuliasis (infection with Linguatul.description: Linguatuliasis is a zoonotic infection caused by a tongue worm, a pentastomid parasite. Humans can acquire infection through contaminated food or contact with infected animals; Spain is within the geographic range of the parasite.

Dirofilariasis (Dirofilaria repens or Di.normalized_text: Dirofilariasis (Dirofilaria repens or Dirofilaria immitis infection)
Dirofilariasis (Dirofilaria repens or Di.description: Dirofilariasis is a mosquito-borne zoonotic filarial nematode infection, usually acquired from canine reservoirs. In humans it commonly presents as a subcutaneous, ocular, or pulmonary nodule containing a worm.

Anisakiasis.description: Anisakiasis is infection by Anisakis larvae after ingestion of raw or undercooked marine fish or squid. It is relatively relevant in Spain because of seafood consumption and can cause acute gastrointestinal or allergic symptoms.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP).description: A progressive neurodegenerative tau disorder characterized by early postural instability, axial rigidity, and supranuclear impairment of vertical eye movements. MRI may show marked midbrain atrophy, sometimes called the hummingbird sign.

Progressive supranuclear palsy with pred.normalized_text: Progressive supranuclear palsy with predominant ocular motor dysfunction (PSP-ocular motor phenotype)
Progressive supranuclear palsy with pred.description: A phenotype of progressive supranuclear palsy in which slowed vertical saccades and vertical supranuclear gaze palsy are the most prominent early manifestations, often before major parkinsonism develops.

Dorsal midbrain syndrome (Parinaud syndr.description: A syndrome caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain, producing impaired vertical gaze, especially upgaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and sometimes abnormal pupillary responses. Causes include tumors, stroke, hydrocephalus, and inflammatory lesions.

Midbrain infarction affecting supranucle.normalized_text: Midbrain infarction affecting supranuclear gaze pathways
Midbrain infarction affecting supranucle.description: An ischemic stroke involving the rostral or dorsal midbrain can disrupt vertical gaze centers and produce vertical gaze palsy, often with additional focal neurologic deficits.

Cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus ne.description: An invasive fungal infection caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeasts, commonly diagnosed in cerebrospinal fluid by India ink staining showing round budding yeasts with prominent clear capsules.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis.description: A lung infection caused by inhalation of Cryptococcus spores; it can remain localized or disseminate to the central nervous system, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: Systemic spread of Cryptococcus infection, potentially involving the bloodstream, lungs, skin, and central nervous system. It is particularly associated with impaired cellular immunity.

Acute pontine ischemic infarction.description: An acute stroke affecting the pons, often due to occlusion of small perforating branches of the basilar artery or vertebrobasilar vascular disease.

Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central.description: Demyelination within the central pons, classically occurring after overly rapid correction of severe hyponatremia or other major osmotic shifts.

Listeria rhombencephalitis.description: A brainstem encephalitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes that can involve the pons, cerebellar peduncles, and cerebellum and may produce focal diffusion abnormalities.

Brainstem demyelinating lesion, includin.normalized_text: Brainstem demyelinating lesion, including multiple sclerosis
Brainstem demyelinating lesion, includin.description: Inflammatory demyelination can produce focal lesions in the pons and other brainstem structures; active lesions can occasionally show restricted diffusion.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (po.normalized_text: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (possibly congenital/neonatal malaria)
Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (po.description: A life-threatening malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, characterized by hemolysis, high parasitemia, thrombocytopenia, and multiple delicate ring forms within individual erythrocytes. In a neonate, this may represent congenital transmission.

Babesiosis.description: A tick-borne protozoal infection caused by Babesia species that infects red blood cells and can produce ring forms, occasionally including tetrad or Maltese-cross forms. Severe disease can cause hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia.

Plasmodium vivax malaria.description: Malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax, usually associated with fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and parasites within red blood cells. Infected erythrocytes are often enlarged and may show Schuffner dots.
