Disseminated cystic echinococcosis (hyda.description: Parasitic infection caused by Echinococcus granulosus, endemic in Mediterranean regions including Spain. It commonly forms cystic lesions in the liver and lungs and can rarely involve the pelvis or other organs; cysts may calcify.

Metastatic malignancy with pulmonary and.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy with pulmonary and hepatic metastases
Metastatic malignancy with pulmonary and.description: Cancer spreading from a primary tumor to distant organs can produce multiple well-circumscribed lung nodules and liver lesions. Possible primary sites include gastrointestinal, gynecologic, renal, thyroid, sarcoma, or melanoma malignancies.

Metastatic pelvic or uterine leiomyoma (.normalized_text: Metastatic pelvic or uterine leiomyoma (benign metastasizing leiomyoma)
Metastatic pelvic or uterine leiomyoma (.description: A rare condition in which smooth-muscle tumors, usually associated with uterine leiomyomas, appear as multiple pulmonary nodules and may involve pelvic or abdominal structures. It is primarily considered in women with a history of uterine fibroids or uterine surgery.

Tuberculosis with pulmonary and extrapul.normalized_text: Tuberculosis with pulmonary and extrapulmonary involvement
Tuberculosis with pulmonary and extrapul.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs, liver, lymph nodes, and pelvis. Chronic lesions may calcify, although the typical lung pattern is usually not multiple large, sharply circumscribed nodules.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease that often affects the lungs and lymph nodes and can involve the liver. Calcified lymph nodes can occur in chronic disease.

Graves disease.description: An autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism characterized by diffuse thyroid enlargement, marked glandular hypervascularity, follicular hyperplasia, and lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.description: A potentially life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis in which potassium shifts into skeletal muscle, causing profound hypokalemia and episodic muscle weakness or paralysis; Graves disease is a common underlying cause.

Hashitoxicosis (transient hyperthyroid p.normalized_text: Hashitoxicosis (transient hyperthyroid phase of autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis)
Hashitoxicosis (transient hyperthyroid p.description: A transient thyrotoxic phase of autoimmune thyroiditis caused by release of preformed thyroid hormone from inflamed thyroid tissue; histology may show prominent lymphocytic infiltration and germinal centers.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign, noncancerous bony overgrowth arising from the midline of the hard palate. It is common, may be lobulated, and is usually found incidentally.

Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.description: A usually benign salivary-gland tumor that can present as a slow-growing, painless, firm mass on the palate, most often on the posterolateral hard palate.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of a minor sali.normalized_text: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of a minor salivary gland
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of a minor sali.description: A malignant salivary-gland tumor that may occur on the palate and can initially appear as a painless, fluctuant or firm swelling; higher-grade tumors may ulcerate or cause pain.

Palatal abscess of odontogenic origin.description: A localized collection of pus from an infected upper tooth that can produce swelling of the palate, usually adjacent to a diseased tooth and often with pain or tenderness.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosi.normalized_text: Degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosis, most severe at L4-L5
Degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosi.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal caused by age-related disc degeneration, facet-joint arthropathy, and ligament thickening; the MRI appearance suggests marked central canal narrowing at L4-L5.

Lumbar degenerative disc disease with di.normalized_text: Lumbar degenerative disc disease with disc bulging/protrusion
Lumbar degenerative disc disease with di.description: Progressive dehydration and degeneration of lumbar intervertebral discs, often with broad-based disc bulges or protrusions that can compress the dural sac or nerve roots.

Degenerative spondylolisthesis at L4-L5.description: Forward slippage of one vertebra relative to the vertebra below due to degeneration of the facet joints and discs; it commonly contributes to lumbar spinal stenosis.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.normalized_text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) with pulmonary arteriovenous malformation and cerebral vascular malformations
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An inherited vascular disorder causing telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, commonly involving the lungs, brain, liver, and nasal mucosa. Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations can permit paradoxical emboli to reach the brain.

Paradoxical cerebral embolism caused by.normalized_text: Paradoxical cerebral embolism caused by a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation
Paradoxical cerebral embolism caused by.description: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation creates a right-to-left shunt, allowing venous thrombi, septic material, or air emboli to bypass the pulmonary capillary filter and embolize to the cerebral circulation.

Cerebral arteriovenous malformation or d.normalized_text: Cerebral arteriovenous malformation or dural arteriovenous fistula
Cerebral arteriovenous malformation or d.description: An abnormal direct connection between arteries and veins in or around the brain can produce enlarged tortuous vessels, venous hypertension, ischemia, and intracranial hemorrhage.

Septic embolic stroke with possible myco.normalized_text: Septic embolic stroke with possible mycotic cerebral aneurysm
Septic embolic stroke with possible myco.description: Infective endocarditis or another bloodstream infection can generate infected emboli that cause multifocal ischemic infarcts, hemorrhage, brain abscesses, and infectious (mycotic) aneurysms.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic inflammatory granulomatous disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often affecting intrathoracic lymph nodes and lungs.

Tuberculosis with mediastinal lymphadeni.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause thoracic lymphadenopathy and granulomatous inflammation; it may be especially considered in endemic settings or with relevant exposure history.

Lymphoma.description: A malignant proliferation of lymphoid cells that can present with mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy and intense FDG uptake on PET imaging.

Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis (adult.normalized_text: Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis (adult osteopetrosis, often type II/Albers-Schönberg disease)
Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis (adult.description: An inherited disorder of impaired osteoclast-mediated bone resorption causing diffusely increased skeletal density, abnormal bone remodeling, and sometimes fractures, osteoarthritis, cranial-nerve compression, or anemia.

Autosomal recessive osteopetrosis.description: A severe inherited osteoclast dysfunction disorder characterized by failure of bone resorption, very dense but brittle bones, narrowing of marrow spaces, and possible bone-marrow failure or neurologic complications.

Osteopetrosis due to carbonic anhydrase.normalized_text: Osteopetrosis due to carbonic anhydrase II deficiency
Osteopetrosis due to carbonic anhydrase.description: A rare autosomal recessive form of osteopetrosis caused by carbonic anhydrase II deficiency, typically associated with osteosclerosis, renal tubular acidosis, and cerebral calcification.

Skeletal fluorosis.description: An acquired metabolic bone disease caused by chronic excess fluoride exposure, producing diffuse osteosclerosis, increased bone density, ligament calcification, joint stiffness, and bone pain.

Paget disease of bone, sclerotic phase.normalized_text: Paget disease of bone, sclerotic phase
Paget disease of bone, sclerotic phase.description: A focal disorder of excessive and disorganized bone remodeling that can produce enlarged, sclerotic bones and elevated bone density in involved regions, particularly the pelvis, spine, skull, and femur.

Intracranial germinoma (suprasellar/hypo.description: A central nervous system germ-cell tumor that commonly involves the suprasellar region, pituitary stalk, hypothalamus, and sometimes pineal region. It can cause central diabetes insipidus, stalk-effect hyperprolactinemia, and anterior panhypopituitarism.

Neurosarcoidosis involving the hypothala.description: Granulomatous inflammation from sarcoidosis can infiltrate the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, pituitary gland, optic pathways, and meninges, producing diabetes insipidus and multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Tuberculous meningitis with hypothalamic.description: Central nervous system tuberculosis can cause chronic basilar meningitis and enhancing granulomas involving the pituitary stalk, hypothalamus, optic chiasm, or adjacent brain structures. Endocrine dysfunction and diabetes insipidus may result.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.normalized_text: Primary central nervous system lymphoma involving the hypothalamus-pituitary region
Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: Primary CNS lymphoma can present as enhancing periventricular, hypothalamic, or suprasellar lesions. Involvement of the pituitary stalk or hypothalamus can cause diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, and hypopituitarism.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypothalamic-pituitary involvement
Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.description: Langerhans cell histiocytosis can infiltrate the posterior pituitary, pituitary stalk, and hypothalamus. Diabetes insipidus is a classic endocrine manifestation, and anterior pituitary deficiencies may develop with more extensive disease.

Partial atrioventricular septal defect (.normalized_text: Partial atrioventricular septal defect (ostium primum atrial septal defect)
Partial atrioventricular septal defect (.description: A congenital defect of the lower interatrial septum associated with abnormal atrioventricular valve anatomy, often including a cleft in the left atrioventricular (mitral) valve. It commonly causes right-sided volume overload and conduction abnormalities.

Ostium secundum atrial septal defect.description: A common congenital opening in the central interatrial septum that allows left-to-right shunting, potentially producing right atrial and right ventricular enlargement and atrial arrhythmias later in life.

Cor triatriatum sinister.description: A rare congenital anomaly in which a membrane divides the left atrium into two chambers, potentially obstructing pulmonary venous drainage and mimicking mitral stenosis.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by severe acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation, especially in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Classic infantile disease causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, weakness, and respiratory failure.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: A milder form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency with residual enzyme activity. It primarily causes progressive proximal skeletal-muscle and respiratory-muscle weakness; clinically significant cardiomyopathy is uncommon.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal/autophagy-related disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency. It can produce severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and intellectual disability, usually affecting boys.

Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leu.description: A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts involving bone marrow and potentially extranodal sites. It commonly expresses B-cell markers such as CD19 and often CD10; aberrant myeloid-marker expression such as CD33 can occur.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that may involve lymph nodes, bone marrow, muscle, kidneys, liver, or other extranodal sites and is typically strongly FDG-avid on PET imaging.

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: A highly aggressive mature germinal-center B-cell neoplasm, usually CD19- and CD10-positive, with frequent extranodal and bone marrow involvement and elevated LDH due to rapid cellular turnover.

Follicular lymphoma with high-grade tran.description: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent germinal-center B-cell lymphoma commonly expressing CD19 and CD10. Transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma can cause rapidly progressive extranodal, marrow, and PET-avid disease with elevated LDH.

B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma with disse.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma with disseminated extranodal involvement
B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma with disse.description: A precursor B-cell neoplasm that is termed lymphoblastic lymphoma when it predominantly forms tissue masses and acute lymphoblastic leukemia when marrow and blood involvement is substantial. It can involve bone, soft tissues, kidneys, and marrow.

Breast cellulitis (non-lactational masti.description: An acute bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue of the breast, causing localized inflammation; ultrasound may show skin thickening and edematous subcutaneous tissue without a drainable abscess.

Erysipelas of the breast.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by streptococci, characterized by rapidly developing red, warm, swollen skin; the borders may be relatively sharp.

Inflammatory breast cancer.description: An aggressive form of breast cancer in which tumor emboli obstruct dermal lymphatic vessels, producing rapid breast redness, swelling, edema, and sometimes peau d'orange changes. It can mimic mastitis or cellulitis.

Breast abscess.description: A localized collection of pus within breast tissue, often developing as a complication of mastitis; it commonly causes focal painful swelling, redness, and a fluctuant mass.

Granulomatous mastitis.description: A chronic inflammatory breast disorder that can produce painful breast swelling, erythema, masses, sinus tracts, or abscess-like lesions and may resemble infection or inflammatory breast cancer.

Dermatomyositis.description: An inflammatory autoimmune myopathy characterized by distinctive photosensitive skin eruptions and, often, proximal muscle weakness.

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus.description: A photosensitive autoimmune skin manifestation of lupus that commonly causes widespread red, scaly, annular, or papulosquamous lesions on sun-exposed areas.

Polymorphous light eruption.description: A delayed abnormal inflammatory reaction to ultraviolet light, producing itchy papules or plaques on newly sun-exposed skin.

Photoallergic or phototoxic contact derm.description: A light-induced skin reaction triggered by ultraviolet exposure together with medications, fragrances, sunscreens, plants, or other topical/systemic agents.

Secondary syphilis.description: The disseminated stage of Treponema pallidum infection, which can produce a generalized papular rash and many variable skin findings.

Multiple keratoacanthomas with koebneriz.description: Keratoacanthomas are rapidly growing crateriform keratinizing skin tumors, often considered within the well-differentiated cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma spectrum. In this case, repeated trauma or surgical excisions may have induced new lesions through an isomorphic (Koebner-like) response.

Multiple self-healing squamous epithelio.description: A rare inherited or sporadic keratoacanthoma syndrome characterized by recurrent multiple keratoacanthoma-like squamous tumors that may involute and leave scars. Lesions can be precipitated by trauma and may occur on sun-exposed limbs.

Generalized eruptive keratoacanthoma of.description: A very rare disorder involving the sudden appearance of many small keratoacanthomas, often numbering in the hundreds or thousands, typically involving widespread skin and sometimes mucosal sites.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.description: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant keratinocyte tumor that may present as a rapidly growing hyperkeratotic, ulcerated, crateriform nodule. Keratoacanthoma-type lesions can be difficult to distinguish histologically and clinically from conventional keratoacanthoma.

Verruca vulgaris (common warts) with sec.normalized_text: Verruca vulgaris (common warts) with secondary irritation or ulceration
Verruca vulgaris (common warts) with sec.description: Common warts are human papillomavirus-associated benign epidermal proliferations, usually presenting as rough hyperkeratotic papules. They can coexist with or mimic keratoacanthomatous lesions.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that commonly produces short-segment, patchy spinal cord lesions, often in the cervical and thoracic cord.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, causing severe optic neuritis and myelitis; spinal lesions are typically longitudinally extensive.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An autoimmune demyelinating disease that can cause optic neuritis, acute myelitis, and brain or spinal cord lesions.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy.description: Spinal cord dysfunction caused by degenerative cervical disc disease, osteophytes, or spinal canal narrowing with chronic cord compression.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.normalized_text: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL) with t(X;14)(q22.3;q11.2) involving IRS4 and TCRA/D
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive precursor T-lymphoid neoplasm characterized by marrow and peripheral-blood infiltration by lymphoblasts. The images show an X;14 rearrangement involving the T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus on chromosome 14 and the IRS4 region on Xq22.3, a rare abnormality associated with T-ALL.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia of ambiguou.normalized_text: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia of ambiguous or initially unclassified lineage
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia of ambiguou.description: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a malignancy of immature lymphoid precursor cells that can heavily involve blood and bone marrow. Definitive lineage assignment requires flow-cytometric immunophenotyping and molecular testing.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoid precursor cells that commonly presents with marrow failure and circulating blasts. It can appear morphologically similar to T-ALL but usually has distinct B-cell immunophenotypic and genetic findings.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).description: Systemic infection by Leishmania parasites, usually transmitted by sandflies. It causes reticuloendothelial involvement with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, marrow suppression, and pancytopenia. Intracellular amastigotes may be seen within macrophages on peripheral-blood or bone-marrow examination.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.normalized_text: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by visceral leishmaniasis
Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infections such as visceral leishmaniasis. Typical findings include fever, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, very high ferritin, splenomegaly, and hemophagocytosis in marrow or other tissues.

Severe disseminated visceral leishmanias.normalized_text: Severe disseminated visceral leishmaniasis with pulmonary involvement
Severe disseminated visceral leishmanias.description: An advanced form of visceral leishmaniasis in which widespread infection and immune dysregulation can involve the lungs in addition to the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It may coexist with HLH and cause respiratory imaging abnormalities.

Cerebral cortical vein thrombosis (a for.normalized_text: Cerebral cortical vein thrombosis (a form of cerebral venous thrombosis)
Cerebral cortical vein thrombosis (a for.description: Blood clot formation in a cortical cerebral vein, which can impair venous drainage and cause venous congestion, infarction, edema, or hemorrhage.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with co.normalized_text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with cortical venous extension
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with co.description: Thrombosis of a dural venous sinus that may extend into cortical veins, producing impaired cerebral venous drainage and secondary cortical lesions.

Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortica.normalized_text: Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortical venous reflux
Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortica.description: An abnormal acquired connection between dural arteries and venous channels that can cause retrograde flow into cortical veins, venous engorgement, edema, and venous infarction.

Venous ischemic infarction secondary to.normalized_text: Venous ischemic infarction secondary to cerebral venous thrombosis
Venous ischemic infarction secondary to.description: Brain injury caused by impaired venous outflow rather than arterial occlusion; lesions often do not conform to a single arterial territory and may coexist with edema or hemorrhage.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: A small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition, most often causing palpable purpura on the lower limbs and sometimes involving the gastrointestinal tract, joints, and kidneys.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (h.description: An inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis of the skin, often triggered by infection, medications, autoimmune disease, or malignancy, causing palpable purpura and petechiae on dependent areas such as the legs.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A systemic ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, and sometimes skin, producing purpura or ulcerative lesions.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis, often associated with hepatitis C infection, autoimmune disease, or lymphoproliferative disorders, commonly presenting with dependent palpable purpura.

Cervical lymphoma.description: A malignant proliferation of lymphocytes, such as Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which can present with enlarged metabolically active cervical lymph nodes.

Metastatic head and neck squamous cell c.normalized_text: Metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma to cervical lymph nodes
Metastatic head and neck squamous cell c.description: Spread of squamous cell carcinoma from the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, or other upper aerodigestive tract sites to regional cervical lymph nodes.

Tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis.description: Infection of cervical lymph nodes by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often causing chronic neck swelling and sometimes necrotic or conglomerate lymph nodes.

Cat-scratch disease lymphadenitis.description: A Bartonella henselae infection, usually following cat exposure or a scratch, that can cause regional tender lymphadenopathy and FDG-avid inflammatory nodes.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic ne.description: A benign self-limited inflammatory lymphadenitis that most often affects cervical lymph nodes and can mimic lymphoma on CT and FDG-PET imaging.

Plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma of the.normalized_text: Plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder
Plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma of the.description: A rare, aggressive variant of urothelial carcinoma in which tumor cells grow as discohesive plasmacytoid or signet-ring-like cells infiltrating the bladder wall.

High-grade urothelial carcinoma with car.normalized_text: High-grade urothelial carcinoma with carcinoma in situ
High-grade urothelial carcinoma with car.description: A malignant tumor arising from bladder urothelium; carcinoma in situ is a flat, high-grade lesion that may coexist with invasive tumor and can produce abnormal fluorescence in situ hybridization findings.

Bladder malakoplakia.description: A chronic granulomatous inflammatory disorder of the bladder, usually associated with impaired macrophage function and recurrent bacterial infection; it may appear as a pale plaque or mass and can mimic cancer.

Bilateral hip osteoarthritis, likely sec.normalized_text: Bilateral hip osteoarthritis, likely secondary to developmental dysplasia of the hip
Bilateral hip osteoarthritis, likely sec.description: Degenerative joint disease of both hips with cartilage loss, joint-space narrowing, femoral-head deformity, and remodeling of the acetabula; developmental hip dysplasia can predispose to early severe bilateral osteoarthritis.

Bilateral femoral head avascular necrosi.normalized_text: Bilateral femoral head avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) with secondary osteoarthritis
Bilateral femoral head avascular necrosi.description: Loss of blood supply to the femoral heads causes bone death, collapse and flattening of the articular surface, followed by progressive degenerative arthritis.

Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the.normalized_text: Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip with chronic subluxation
Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the.description: A congenital or developmental abnormality in which the acetabula are shallow and the femoral heads are insufficiently covered, potentially causing chronic partial displacement and early degenerative damage.

Inflammatory arthritis involving both hi.normalized_text: Inflammatory arthritis involving both hips, such as rheumatoid arthritis
Inflammatory arthritis involving both hi.description: Chronic systemic inflammatory arthritis can cause bilateral symmetric hip joint-space loss, erosive remodeling, and progressive destruction of the femoral heads and acetabula.

Patella alta.description: An abnormally high position of the patella relative to the femur and tibia, which can predispose to patellofemoral instability and anterior knee pain.

Patellofemoral instability with lateral.normalized_text: Patellofemoral instability with lateral patellar subluxation
Patellofemoral instability with lateral.description: A tendency of the kneecap to move partially or completely out of the trochlear groove, usually laterally; patella alta is an important predisposing factor.

Patellar tendon rupture.description: A tear of the tendon connecting the patella to the tibial tubercle. A complete rupture commonly produces patella alta on radiographs and inability to actively extend the knee.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A rare, usually low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor that most often occurs in young women. It commonly forms a well-circumscribed pancreatic mass and typically shows nuclear beta-catenin/cyclin D1 staining with expression of vimentin and CD10.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A tumor arising from pancreatic endocrine cells; it may be functional or nonfunctional and often appears as a hypervascular pancreatic mass. Diagnosis is usually supported by synaptophysin and chromogranin expression.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: An uncommon malignant exocrine pancreatic tumor composed of cells with acinar differentiation. It may present as a large pancreatic mass and is typically positive for pancreatic enzyme markers such as trypsin, chymotrypsin, or BCL10.

Gluteal arteriovenous malformation.description: A congenital or acquired high-flow abnormal connection between arteries and veins, producing a vascular mass that can enlarge over time and may be supplied by branches of the internal iliac artery.

Intramuscular hemangioma (venous malform.description: A benign vascular lesion involving muscle or subcutaneous tissue that may appear as a soft mass with bluish skin discoloration and can contain dilated vascular channels or phleboliths.

Hypervascular soft-tissue tumor, such as.normalized_text: Hypervascular soft-tissue tumor, such as an extra-adrenal paraganglioma
Hypervascular soft-tissue tumor, such as.description: Paragangliomas are uncommon neuroendocrine tumors that can arise outside the adrenal glands and are typically highly vascular; some produce catecholamines and can be detected with functional nuclear imaging.

Lateral tibial plateau fracture.description: A fracture involving the upper outer surface of the tibia at the knee joint, sometimes with depression of the weight-bearing articular surface.

Proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture ext.normalized_text: Proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture extending toward the tibial plateau
Proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture ext.description: A fracture of the upper tibia that may extend from the metaphysis into the knee joint surface and can occur after trauma.

Post-traumatic knee osteoarthritis.description: Degenerative cartilage and joint changes that can develop after a prior knee injury, especially after an intra-articular fracture.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Desmoid-type fibromatosis.description: A benign but locally infiltrative fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumor, often composed of bland spindle cells in long fascicles and associated with activating CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations.

Leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma.description: Smooth-muscle tumors composed of intersecting fascicles of spindle cells; leiomyoma is benign, whereas leiomyosarcoma shows significant atypia, mitoses, and/or necrosis.

Nodular fasciitis.description: A benign, rapidly growing reactive or neoplastic myofibroblastic proliferation that may resemble sarcoma histologically but usually has a short clinical course and USP6 rearrangement.

SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1-related disorder).description: A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by PIK3R1 variants, characterized by short stature, partial lipodystrophy, a progeroid facial appearance, delayed dentition, and sometimes insulin resistance or eye abnormalities.

Mandibuloacral dysplasia with lipodystro.description: A laminopathy-related progeroid disorder featuring growth failure, craniofacial abnormalities, mandibular hypoplasia, delayed dentition, skeletal abnormalities, and partial or generalized lipodystrophy.

Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome.description: A rare neonatal progeroid syndrome marked by growth failure, lipoatrophy, aged appearance, sparse scalp hair, craniofacial abnormalities, delayed dentition, and developmental difficulties of variable severity.

Hallermann-Streiff syndrome.description: A congenital craniofacial disorder with a bird-like facial appearance, mandibular hypoplasia, dental anomalies, hypotrichosis, skin atrophy, and sometimes proportionate short stature.

Russell-Silver syndrome.description: A growth-restriction syndrome characterized by low birth weight or postnatal growth failure, triangular face, relative frontal prominence, feeding difficulty, body asymmetry in some patients, and delayed bone age.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A primary antibody-deficiency disorder characterized by low immunoglobulins, impaired antibody responses, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and frequent bronchiectasis. B-cell counts may be reduced, although complete near-absence is less typical.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agam.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by failure of B-cell maturation, resulting in profoundly reduced or absent circulating B cells and severe hypogammaglobulinemia. Recurrent bacterial respiratory infections can lead to bronchiectasis.

Good syndrome (thymoma-associated immuno.description: An adult-onset immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, very low or absent peripheral B cells, and variable T-cell abnormalities, particularly low CD4+ cells.

Late-onset combined immunodeficiency (LO.normalized_text: Late-onset combined immunodeficiency (LOCID), a severe CVID-like disorder
Late-onset combined immunodeficiency (LO.description: A severe adult-onset primary immunodeficiency with impaired antibody production plus significant T-cell deficiency. It often presents with recurrent respiratory infections, bronchiectasis, opportunistic infections, and low CD4+ T-cell counts.

Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia due to B.normalized_text: Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia due to B-cell-depleting therapy (for example, rituximab)
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia due to B.description: Anti-CD20 therapies can cause profound depletion of circulating B cells, reduced immunoglobulins, recurrent respiratory infections, and, when prolonged, bronchiectasis.

Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.normalized_text: Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy)
Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.description: A rare non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder characterized by accumulation of S100-positive histiocytes, often showing emperipolesis (intact lymphocytes within histiocyte cytoplasm). It can involve mediastinal lymph nodes and extranodal sites.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that commonly causes bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and may involve the lungs, skin, eyes, and other organs.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A clonal histiocytic neoplasm involving Langerhans cells, usually identified by CD1a and langerin positivity and often associated with eosinophils and cystic or nodular lung disease.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that commonly presents with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, particularly in young adults, and may cause constitutional symptoms.

Takotsubo syndrome (stress-induced cardi.description: Transient acute left-ventricular systolic dysfunction, often triggered by major physical or emotional stress, which can mimic acute myocardial infarction despite unobstructed coronary arteries.

Acute myocardial infarction with nonobst.normalized_text: Acute myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA), including coronary vasospasm
Acute myocardial infarction with nonobst.description: Myocardial infarction caused by ischemia without a persistently obstructive epicardial coronary lesion; potential mechanisms include transient coronary vasospasm, embolism, spontaneous reperfusion, or microvascular dysfunction.

Acute myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the heart muscle, commonly viral or immune-mediated, which can cause ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmia, myocardial injury-marker elevation, and sudden cardiac arrest with normal coronary arteries.

Massive pulmonary embolism with acute ri.normalized_text: Massive pulmonary embolism with acute right-heart strain
Massive pulmonary embolism with acute ri.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by thrombus can cause acute right-ventricular failure, hypoxemia, shock, myocardial injury-marker elevation, and cardiac arrest.

Chronic portal vein thrombosis with cave.normalized_text: Chronic portal vein thrombosis with cavernous transformation
Chronic portal vein thrombosis with cave.description: Long-standing obstruction of the portal vein by thrombus, with development of multiple small collateral vessels around the porta hepatis (portal cavernoma). Doppler ultrasound may show altered, turbulent, or collateral portal flow, and CT may show portal venous calcification or chronic thrombus.

Portal hypertension due to chronic liver.normalized_text: Portal hypertension due to chronic liver disease or portal venous obstruction
Portal hypertension due to chronic liver.description: Elevated pressure in the portal venous system, commonly caused by cirrhosis or chronic portal vein obstruction. It can produce collateral vessels, impaired hepatic detoxification, coagulopathy, and elevated ammonia.

Arterioportal fistula.description: An abnormal communication between a hepatic or splanchnic artery and the portal venous system. Doppler imaging can demonstrate turbulent, high-velocity, pulsatile, or arterialized flow within the portal vein and may lead to portal hypertension.

Mesenteric venous thrombosis with extens.normalized_text: Mesenteric venous thrombosis with extension to the portal venous system
Mesenteric venous thrombosis with extens.description: Thrombosis involving the superior mesenteric vein and/or portal vein can impair intestinal and portal venous drainage. Chronic disease can develop collateral circulation and portal hypertension; acute disease may cause abdominal pain and bowel ischemia.

Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.normalized_text: Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis
Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.description: An expanding annular erythematous rash caused by Borrelia infection after a tick bite. Multiple lesions can occur in early disseminated Lyme disease; Lyme borreliosis is present in Spain.

Tinea corporis (ringworm).description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection that produces round or annular plaques, often with a more active red edge and central clearing.

Erythema multiforme.description: An immune-mediated eruption characterized by target lesions, often triggered by infections or medications and commonly involving the extremities.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory skin condition causing smooth annular plaques formed by grouped papules, usually without scale.

Infectious aortitis with mycotic abdomin.normalized_text: Infectious aortitis with mycotic abdominal aortic pseudoaneurysm
Infectious aortitis with mycotic abdomin.description: Infection of the aortic wall can cause inflammation, wall destruction, and a rapidly enlarging saccular pseudoaneurysm. Potential pathogens in Spain include Salmonella species, Staphylococcus aureus, Coxiella burnetii, and Brucella species.

Abdominal aortic intramural hematoma or.normalized_text: Abdominal aortic intramural hematoma or penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer
Abdominal aortic intramural hematoma or.description: An intramural hematoma is bleeding within the aortic wall, while a penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer is an ulcerated atherosclerotic plaque that extends into the media. Either can progress to focal pseudoaneurysm or rupture.

Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm /.normalized_text: Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm / chronic periaortitis
Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm /.description: Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm is an aneurysm associated with dense periaortic inflammation and fibrosis. It can overlap with IgG4-related disease and may cause pain or obstruction of nearby structures.

Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastri.normalized_text: Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastric pouch and transverse colon
Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastri.description: An abnormal communication between the stomach (in this case the gastric pouch) and the colon. The contrast study directly demonstrates passage between the gastric pouch and transverse colon.

Post-bariatric surgery gastrocolic fistu.description: A gastrocolic fistula can occur as a late complication of bariatric surgery, particularly after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, often related to marginal ulceration, staple-line problems, or local inflammation.

Marginal ulcer with fistulization to the.normalized_text: Marginal ulcer with fistulization to the colon
Marginal ulcer with fistulization to the.description: A marginal ulcer is an ulcer near a gastrojejunal anastomosis or gastric pouch after gastric surgery. Deep ulceration and inflammation can rarely erode into adjacent colon and form a gastrocolic fistula.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), likely chronic bronchitis phenotype
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.description: A chronic airflow-limiting lung disease, commonly associated with smoking or environmental exposures. Chest radiographs may show hyperinflation and increased bronchovascular/peribronchial markings.

Asthma.description: A chronic inflammatory airway disorder causing episodic, usually reversible airway obstruction. Chest radiographs can be normal or show mild hyperinflation and peribronchial thickening.

Acute or chronic bronchitis.description: Inflammation of the bronchi, often caused by viral infection, irritant exposure, or smoking. Radiographs may show increased peribronchial markings but often do not show a focal infiltrate.

Pellagra (niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency).description: A nutritional deficiency disorder caused by inadequate niacin or tryptophan. It can cause photosensitive dermatitis, classically involving the neck (Casal necklace) and sun-exposed hands and forearms.

Photocontact dermatitis / photodermatiti.description: An inflammatory skin reaction triggered or worsened by ultraviolet exposure, sometimes after contact with medications, fragrances, plants, or sunscreens.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder affecting skin and muscle. Characteristic cutaneous features include photosensitive rashes of the neck and upper chest and papules over the knuckles.

Chronic eczematous dermatitis (atopic or.normalized_text: Chronic eczematous dermatitis (atopic or contact dermatitis)
Chronic eczematous dermatitis (atopic or.description: A common inflammatory skin condition characterized by itching, redness, scaling, excoriations, and skin thickening; it may be caused by atopy, irritants, or allergens.

Agmaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X (.normalized_text: Agmaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X (XLA; Agammaglobulinemia de Bruton)
Agmaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X (.description: Una inmunodeficiencia primaria causada por variantes patógenas de BTK que dificultan la maduración de las células B, resultando en una reducción notable de inmunoglobulinas y susceptibilidad a infecciones bacterianas y enterovirales recurrentes tras el deterioro de los anticuerpos maternos.

Agammaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X.normalized_text: Agammaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X relacionada con BTK debido al mosaicismo somático/gonadal materno
Agammaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X.description: Agammaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X en un niño varón causada por una variante patogénica BTK heredada de una madre con mosaicismo somático de bajo nivel; el mosaicismo también puede implicar posible afectación de la línea germinal y riesgo de recurrencia.

Inmunodeficiencia variable común (CVID).description: Un trastorno heterogéneo de deficiencia de anticuerpos caracterizado por una reducción de IgG con bajas IgA y/o IgM y respuestas de anticuerpos deterioradas, que a menudo se presenta con infecciones respiratorias y gastrointestinales recurrentes; generalmente se diagnostica más tarde en la infancia o la edad adulta.

Hipogammaglobulinemia transitoria de la.description: Un retraso temporal en la maduración de la producción de inmunoglobulinas durante la infancia, que suele implicar bajos niveles de IgG y, a veces, bajos de IgA o IgM, con eventual normalización espontánea.

Penile fracture (rupture of the right co.normalized_text: Penile fracture (rupture of the right corpus cavernosum tunica albuginea)
Penile fracture (rupture of the right co.description: An acute tear of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually caused by blunt bending trauma to the erect penis, with associated hemorrhage.

Penile soft-tissue hematoma due to traum.normalized_text: Penile soft-tissue hematoma due to traumatic corporal injury
Penile soft-tissue hematoma due to traum.description: A collection of blood in penile and/or scrotal soft tissues after trauma; it may accompany a penile fracture or occur with less severe soft-tissue injury.

Isolated corpus cavernosum injury.description: Traumatic injury to erectile tissue of a corpus cavernosum, potentially causing localized bleeding and hematoma; if the tunica albuginea is disrupted, it is classified as penile fracture.

Enfermedad músculo-ojo-cerebro (disstrog.description: Una distrofia muscular congénita autosómica-recesiva causada por variantes patógenas en POMGNT1, que afecta la glicosilación alfa-destroglicano. Comúnmente causa malformaciones cerebrales, anomalías oculares y afectación muscular. POMGNT1 se localiza en la región del cromosoma 1 reportada, y la ausencia o reducción de la cobertura de exones es compatible con una posible deleción de exones.

Síndrome de Walker-Warburg.description: Una distrofalopatía congénita grave, generalmente debida a defectos en genes implicados en la glicosilación alfa-destroglicana, incluyendo POMGNT1. Se caracteriza por distrofia muscular congénita, malformaciones cerebrales severas, hidrocefalia y grandes anomalías oculares.

Distrofia-dicoglicanopatía muscular cong.normalized_text: Distrofia-dicoglicanopatía muscular congénita relacionada con POMGNT1, tipo A3
Distrofia-dicoglicanopatía muscular cong.description: Una disgustanopatía grave asociada a POMGNT1 caracterizada por anomalías estructurales cerebrales, hidrocefalia o ventricularomegalia, anomalías oculares y distrofia muscular congénita. Esta categoría incluye el extremo grave del espectro de la enfermedad POMGNT1.

Distrofia y distrombopatía muscular de c.normalized_text: Distrofia y distrombopatía muscular de cintura articular relacionada con POMGNT1, tipo C3
Distrofia y distrombopatía muscular de c.description: Una distoglicanopatía relacionada con POMGNT1 más leve que puede presentarse con debilidad muscular de la cintura membre, discapacidad intelectual variable y anomalías cerebrales y oculares menos graves o ausentes en comparación con la enfermedad músculo-ojo-cerebro.

Prostatic adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from prostatic glandular cells; it commonly forms infiltrative small glands and can be supported by prostate-marker immunostaining such as PSA, PSAP, or NKX3.1.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or p.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or prostatic urethra with glandular differentiation
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or p.description: A malignant tumor arising from the urothelial lining of the bladder or urethra. Some tumors show glandular differentiation and can involve the prostate or present as a pelvic mass.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic ex.normalized_text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic extension or invasion of the prostate
Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic ex.description: A gland-forming malignant tumor of the colon or rectum that can invade adjacent pelvic structures, including the prostate, seminal vesicles, bladder, or pelvic soft tissues.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, an elevated osmolality gap early after exposure, and possible acute kidney injury due to toxic metabolites and calcium oxalate deposition.

Methanol poisoning.description: Methanol ingestion produces toxic formate metabolites, causing severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and an increased osmolality gap, particularly early in poisoning.

Propylene glycol toxicity.description: Propylene glycol exposure, often from intravenous medications such as lorazepam, diazepam, phenobarbital, or some formulations of nitroglycerin, can cause elevated osmolality gap, lactic acidosis, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and kidney dysfunction.

Metformin-associated lactic acidosis.description: A rare complication of metformin accumulation, usually in renal impairment, hypoperfusion, sepsis, or overdose, characterized by marked lactic acidosis and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Diethylene glycol poisoning.description: Diethylene glycol ingestion is a toxic alcohol exposure that can produce an elevated osmolality gap early, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, lactic acidosis, and progressive acute kidney injury.

diagnoses.name: Juvenile granulosa-cell tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site

Pelvic malakoplakia.description: A rare chronic granulomatous inflammatory disorder caused by impaired macrophage bacterial killing, most often associated with Escherichia coli infection. It can form a large pelvic or abdominopelvic mass and mimic a gynecologic malignancy. Histology typically shows sheets of macrophages with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.

Xanthogranulomatous salpingo-oophoritis.description: A destructive chronic inflammatory disease of the ovary and fallopian tube, often related to chronic pelvic infection. It produces a large solid-cystic pelvic mass with foamy macrophages, abscesses, fibrosis, and inflammatory cells, frequently resembling ovarian cancer radiologically.

Pelvic actinomycosis.description: A chronic invasive infection caused by Actinomyces species that can create infiltrative pelvic masses, abscesses, fibrosis, and adhesions. It commonly mimics advanced ovarian or pelvic malignancy and is particularly associated with long-term intrauterine-device use.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma with inflam.normalized_text: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma with inflammatory response
Epithelial ovarian carcinoma with inflam.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the ovary that may present as a large pelvic mass and can cause anemia and elevated inflammatory markers. Necrosis, tumor-associated inflammation, or superinfection can produce leukocytosis and high CRP.

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

Hemoglobin H disease (alpha-thalassemia.description: A form of alpha-thalassemia caused by loss or dysfunction of three alpha-globin genes, leading to excess beta-globin tetramers (hemoglobin H), chronic microcytic hemolytic anemia, and characteristic hemoglobin H inclusion bodies on supravital staining.

Nondeletional hemoglobin H disease (for.normalized_text: Nondeletional hemoglobin H disease (for example, hemoglobin H–Constant Spring disease)
Nondeletional hemoglobin H disease (for.description: A generally more severe subtype of hemoglobin H disease in which an alpha-globin gene deletion is combined with a nondeletional alpha-globin mutation, often causing more marked chronic anemia, hemolysis, and growth or skeletal effects.

Beta-thalassemia major or severe beta-th.normalized_text: Beta-thalassemia major or severe beta-thalassemia intermedia
Beta-thalassemia major or severe beta-th.description: Inherited reduced or absent beta-globin production causing severe chronic microcytic anemia; untreated severe disease can produce marrow expansion and characteristic facial bone changes.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Orm.description: A fibro-inflammatory disorder causing plaque-like soft tissue in the retroperitoneum, typically around the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels, often entrapping and medially displacing the ureters.

IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: An immune-mediated form of retroperitoneal fibrosis associated with IgG4-related disease. It can produce a periaortic soft-tissue mantle and cause ureteral obstruction.

Retroperitoneal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma may present with retroperitoneal nodal masses that surround major vessels and can compress the ureters, producing obstructive uropathy.

Metastatic retroperitoneal malignancy or.description: Metastatic cancer involving retroperitoneal lymph nodes or soft tissues can encase ureters and vessels, causing hydronephrosis or ureteral obstruction.

Right-sided community-acquired pneumonia.description: Acute infection of lung parenchyma causing alveolar consolidation, which may involve one or more lobes and can produce near-complete opacification of a hemithorax when extensive.

Post-obstructive pneumonia with right-lu.description: Lung collapse and secondary infection distal to obstruction of a major bronchus, commonly caused by mucus impaction, an aspirated foreign body, or an endobronchial tumor.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the lungs that can cause segmental consolidation, airway spread, cavitation, lymph-node enlargement, and lobar collapse from bronchial involvement.

Fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder causing alternating areas of narrowing and dilation, classically producing a 'string-of-beads' appearance on angiography. It may affect renal, carotid, vertebral, visceral, and iliac arteries.

Segmental arterial mediolysis.description: A rare noninflammatory arteriopathy of medium-to-large abdominal arteries characterized by arterial dissections, stenoses, aneurysms, and alternating dilatation and narrowing, often involving visceral vessels.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can produce microaneurysms, stenoses, occlusions, and irregular beading of renal, mesenteric, hepatic, and other visceral arteries.

Sustained monomorphic ventricular tachyc.description: A potentially life-threatening rapid rhythm originating in the ventricles, producing a regular broad-complex tachycardia.

Supraventricular tachycardia with aberra.normalized_text: Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant intraventricular conduction
Supraventricular tachycardia with aberra.description: A rapid rhythm arising above the ventricles that appears wide on ECG because of bundle-branch block or other abnormal ventricular conduction.

Antidromic atrioventricular re-entrant t.normalized_text: Antidromic atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia due to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Antidromic atrioventricular re-entrant t.description: A re-entrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway to activate the ventricles, causing a regular broad-complex tachycardia.

Fetal ventriculomegaly.description: Abnormal enlargement of the fetal cerebral ventricles due to increased cerebrospinal-fluid volume; it may be isolated or associated with other brain, genetic, or infectious conditions.

Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congeni.normalized_text: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congenital aqueductal stenosis
Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congeni.description: A blockage or narrowing of the cerebral aqueduct can prevent cerebrospinal-fluid drainage, causing dilation of the lateral and third ventricles, often with relative sparing of the fourth ventricle.

Dandy-Walker malformation.description: A congenital posterior-fossa malformation characterized by cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle, abnormal development of the cerebellar vermis, and frequently associated ventriculomegaly.

Agenesis of the corpus callosum with ven.normalized_text: Agenesis of the corpus callosum with ventriculomegaly
Agenesis of the corpus callosum with ven.description: Partial or complete absence of the corpus callosum can alter ventricular shape and cause colpocephaly, with disproportionate enlargement of the posterior portions of the lateral ventricles.

Primary pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Initial infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often producing a pulmonary focus with hilar or mediastinal lymph-node enlargement and caseating granulomas containing multinucleated giant cells.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that commonly affects the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes, classically causing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and noncaseating granulomas.

Pulmonary fungal infection with granulom.normalized_text: Pulmonary fungal infection with granulomatous lymphadenitis
Pulmonary fungal infection with granulom.description: Certain fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, can produce pulmonary infiltrates, hilar lymph-node enlargement, and necrotizing granulomas that resemble tuberculosis.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary i.description: Infection by mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis can cause chronic pulmonary disease and granulomatous inflammation, sometimes with necrosis and lymph-node involvement.

Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).normalized_text: Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear or degeneration
Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).description: Injury or degenerative wear of the fibrocartilage and ligaments on the ulnar side of the wrist, often involving the central articular disc.

Degenerative central perforation of the.normalized_text: Degenerative central perforation of the TFCC
Degenerative central perforation of the.description: A wear-related defect in the central portion of the triangular fibrocartilage disc, more common with aging, repetitive wrist loading, or ulnar-sided mechanical stress.

Ulnar impaction syndrome.description: A condition in which excessive loading between the ulna, TFCC, lunate, and triquetrum causes degeneration or tearing of the TFCC and adjacent cartilage or bone.

Lunotriquetral ligament injury.description: Sprain, partial tear, or complete tear of the ligament connecting the lunate and triquetrum, which may cause ulnar-sided wrist pain and carpal instability.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with bil.normalized_text: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with bilateral corticospinal tract injury
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with bil.description: Brain injury caused by reduced oxygen delivery or cerebral blood flow, which can produce symmetric diffusion restriction in the internal capsules, corona radiata, and corticospinal tracts.

Bilateral internal watershed ischemic in.description: Ischemic injury in border-zone regions between major cerebral arterial territories, often associated with systemic hypoperfusion and sometimes affecting bilateral deep white matter.

Acute bilateral ischemic stroke affectin.normalized_text: Acute bilateral ischemic stroke affecting perforator or medullary arterial territories
Acute bilateral ischemic stroke affectin.description: Acute infarction due to impaired blood flow in small penetrating or medullary cerebral arteries; bilateral lesions can occur with systemic vascular, embolic, or metabolic contributors.

Wallerian degeneration secondary to an a.normalized_text: Wallerian degeneration secondary to an acute cerebral injury
Wallerian degeneration secondary to an a.description: Degeneration of descending nerve fibers after injury to upstream motor pathways; early stages can show diffusion restriction along the corticospinal tracts.

Hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.description: A rare vascular tumor of the liver composed of epithelioid endothelial cells, often presenting as multiple liver lesions with variable peripheral or delayed enhancement.

Hepatic hemangioma.description: A benign vascular malformation of the liver and the most common benign hepatic tumor; it may appear hyperechoic on ultrasound and show peripheral nodular enhancement on CT.

Hepatic angiomyolipoma.description: A rare benign mesenchymal liver tumor composed of variable amounts of blood vessels, smooth-muscle-like epithelioid cells, and fat; some lesions have little visible fat and can mimic malignancy.

Hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor arising from hepatocytes, usually associated with cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B or C infection, or other chronic liver disease; it commonly demonstrates arterial enhancement on multiphasic CT.

Hepatic metastases.description: Secondary malignant deposits in the liver from a cancer elsewhere in the body; metastases commonly present as multiple liver lesions with variable contrast enhancement patterns.

Lupus panniculitis (lupus erythematosus.normalized_text: Lupus panniculitis (lupus erythematosus profundus) of the scalp
Lupus panniculitis (lupus erythematosus.description: A chronic cutaneous lupus manifestation involving subcutaneous fat, causing lymphocytic lobular panniculitis, fat necrosis, atrophy, and potentially permanent scarring alopecia when the scalp is affected.

Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell ly.description: A rare cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in which neoplastic cytotoxic T cells infiltrate subcutaneous fat, often mimicking inflammatory panniculitis and occasionally producing alopecic or atrophic lesions.

Traumatic panniculitis with secondary sc.normalized_text: Traumatic panniculitis with secondary scarring alopecia
Traumatic panniculitis with secondary sc.description: Inflammation and necrosis of subcutaneous fat caused by local pressure, physical trauma, injections, or repeated mechanical injury; healing can leave atrophy and loss of hair when it affects the scalp.

Morphea profunda (deep localized sclerod.normalized_text: Morphea profunda (deep localized scleroderma) of the scalp
Morphea profunda (deep localized sclerod.description: A localized sclerosing connective-tissue disorder that can extend into subcutaneous tissue, producing skin tightening, atrophy, and sometimes scarring alopecia when affecting the scalp.

Small-bowel intussusception.description: Telescoping of one segment of small bowel into another, which can cause intermittent or acute intestinal obstruction. CT may show a target or bowel-within-bowel appearance.

Crohn disease with inflammatory small-bo.normalized_text: Crohn disease with inflammatory small-bowel stricture and obstruction
Crohn disease with inflammatory small-bo.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect the small intestine, causing segmental bowel-wall thickening, strictures, obstruction, and occasionally intussusception.

Small-bowel obstruction due to retained.normalized_text: Small-bowel obstruction due to retained capsule endoscope or other intraluminal foreign body
Small-bowel obstruction due to retained.description: Mechanical obstruction can occur when a capsule endoscope or other foreign body becomes lodged at a pre-existing narrowing, such as a stricture from Crohn disease, tumor, or adhesions.

Small-bowel lymphoma or other small-bowe.normalized_text: Small-bowel lymphoma or other small-bowel neoplasm causing a lead point for intussusception
Small-bowel lymphoma or other small-bowe.description: A benign or malignant bowel lesion can act as a lead point for adult intussusception and may produce bowel obstruction, wall thickening, or a mass-like target appearance on CT.

Myocardial bridging of the left anterior.normalized_text: Myocardial bridging of the left anterior descending coronary artery with acute coronary syndrome
Myocardial bridging of the left anterior.description: A congenital intramyocardial course of a coronary segment, most often the mid-left anterior descending artery, causing systolic compression ('milking') of the vessel and potentially myocardial ischemia or infarction.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) related to myocardial bridging
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute myocardial infarction without persistent ST-segment elevation, diagnosed by a rise in cardiac troponin with evidence of myocardial ischemia; in this case, dynamic LAD compression from myocardial bridging is a plausible mechanism.

Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease that commonly affects renal and carotid arteries and produces alternating stenosis and dilation, often described as a 'string-of-beads' appearance on angiography or CT.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.normalized_text: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) associated with fibromuscular dysplasia
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: A nonatherosclerotic separation of layers in the coronary arterial wall that can cause acute coronary syndrome. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a recognized associated arteriopathy, and extracoronary vascular imaging may show renal artery beading.

Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).description: Retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into one or both ureters and renal collecting systems, often identified on a voiding cystourethrogram.

High-grade vesicoureteral reflux with hy.description: Severe VUR can cause dilatation and tortuosity of the ureter and dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces, increasing the risk of recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scarring.

Posterior urethral valves.description: A congenital obstructing membrane in the posterior urethra of male infants and children that can cause bladder outlet obstruction, bladder changes, hydroureteronephrosis, and secondary vesicoureteral reflux.

Neurogenic bladder with secondary vesico.normalized_text: Neurogenic bladder with secondary vesicoureteral reflux
Neurogenic bladder with secondary vesico.description: Impaired bladder innervation can lead to poor bladder emptying, elevated bladder pressure, urinary retention, recurrent infections, and reflux into the ureters.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by muscle inflammation, characteristic skin manifestations, and microvascular injury. Severe cases can cause prominent facial edema and involvement of pharyngeal, tongue, and neck muscles.

Trichinellosis.description: A parasitic infection caused by Trichinella species after ingestion of undercooked infected meat. Larval migration into skeletal muscle causes myositis, edema, and classically periorbital swelling.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory myositis
Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause rash, edema, small-vessel inflammation, and inflammatory muscle disease; lupus-associated myositis may resemble dermatomyositis.

Infectious myositis or cellulitis of the.normalized_text: Infectious myositis or cellulitis of the deep facial and neck spaces
Infectious myositis or cellulitis of the.description: Bacterial infection of soft tissues or muscle can produce localized edema, pain, erythema, and swelling of facial, oral-floor, and neck structures; severe cases may threaten the airway.

Impetigo (nonbullous impetigo).description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, characterized by erosions and classic honey-colored crusts.

Bullous impetigo.description: A toxin-mediated Staphylococcus aureus skin infection in which fragile superficial blisters rupture, leaving moist erosions with yellow-brown crusting and collarettes of scale.

Impetiginized dermatitis (infected eczem.normalized_text: Impetiginized dermatitis (infected eczema or contact dermatitis)
Impetiginized dermatitis (infected eczem.description: An inflammatory dermatitis that has developed secondary bacterial infection, producing weeping erosions, redness, and honey-colored crusts.

Cutaneous larva migrans with secondary b.normalized_text: Cutaneous larva migrans with secondary bacterial infection
Cutaneous larva migrans with secondary b.description: A skin infestation caused by migrating hookworm larvae, producing winding, serpiginous tracks; scratching or skin breakdown may lead to secondary impetigo.

Chronic tophaceous gout.description: Advanced gout caused by long-term deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues, forming large nodules called tophi and causing deforming arthritis.

Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis.description: A rare systemic histiocytic disorder characterized by papulonodular skin lesions and severe, potentially mutilating erosive polyarthritis, often involving the hands.

Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nod.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis that commonly causes symmetric hand and wrist synovitis, joint deformity, and occasionally firm subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules.

Calcinosis cutis associated with systemi.normalized_text: Calcinosis cutis associated with systemic sclerosis or dermatomyositis
Calcinosis cutis associated with systemi.description: Deposition of calcium salts in skin and soft tissue, which can produce hard periarticular nodules, ulceration, restricted movement, and hand deformity in connective-tissue diseases.

Thymoma.description: A tumor arising from thymic epithelial cells, usually presenting as a well-defined anterior mediastinal mass in adults. It may be associated with myasthenia gravis or other autoimmune disorders.

Mediastinal lymphoma.description: Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve mediastinal lymph nodes and create an anterior mediastinal mass, sometimes with bulky nodal enlargement.

Substernal thyroid goiter or ectopic thy.normalized_text: Substernal thyroid goiter or ectopic thyroid tissue
Substernal thyroid goiter or ectopic thy.description: Enlarged thyroid tissue can extend into the superior anterior mediastinum, often appearing as a heterogeneous soft-tissue mass contiguous with the cervical thyroid.

Mediastinal germ-cell tumor.description: Germ-cell tumors, including teratoma and seminoma, may arise in the anterior mediastinum. Teratomas may contain fat, fluid, calcification, or soft tissue.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis (stage II).description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that commonly causes bilateral hilar lymph-node enlargement and interstitial or perihilar lung infiltrates.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: An infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can produce hilar lymphadenopathy and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, particularly in primary or disseminated disease.

Atypical or viral bronchopneumonia.description: Respiratory infection causing bilateral patchy or interstitial pulmonary opacities, often centered around the hila or lower lungs.

Lymphoma with thoracic lymph-node involv.description: A malignancy of lymphoid tissue that can cause mediastinal or hilar lymph-node enlargement and may produce secondary pulmonary infiltrates.

Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis.description: Tumor spread through pulmonary lymphatic vessels, most often from lung, breast, stomach, pancreas, prostate, or other metastatic cancer. It commonly produces interlobular septal and peribronchovascular thickening.

Unilateral pulmonary edema.description: Fluid accumulation in the lung interstitium and airspaces, usually from cardiac dysfunction or localized pulmonary venous obstruction. It can occasionally be unilateral, particularly with mitral regurgitation or pulmonary vein stenosis.

Pulmonary vein stenosis or obstruction.description: Narrowing or blockage of a pulmonary vein can cause localized venous hypertension and unilateral pulmonary edema-like changes. It may occur after atrial fibrillation ablation, from mediastinal fibrosis, thrombus, or tumor compression.

Infectious bronchiolitis or atypical pne.description: Small-airway infection or atypical pulmonary infection can produce centrilobular nodules, branching linear opacities, peribronchial thickening, and patchy unilateral interstitial infiltrates.

Right diaphragmatic eventration.description: Congenital or acquired thinning and abnormal elevation of an intact hemidiaphragm, commonly affecting the right side and potentially compressing adjacent lung.

Right unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis.description: Loss of diaphragmatic movement due to phrenic nerve dysfunction, producing persistent elevation of one hemidiaphragm and possible reduced ventilation at the lung base.

Right basilar compressive atelectasis se.normalized_text: Right basilar compressive atelectasis secondary to elevated diaphragm
Right basilar compressive atelectasis se.description: Partial collapse or underexpansion of the lower lung caused by external compression or reduced diaphragmatic excursion.

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-center B-cell type
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that can arise in extranodal sites, including the oral cavity and maxilla. The large atypical lymphoid cells and expression of CD10 and BCL6 support germinal-center differentiation; MUM1 can also be expressed.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma.description: A category of aggressive mature B-cell lymphomas, often presenting as rapidly enlarging extranodal masses and requiring MYC, BCL2, and BCL6 testing to identify rearranged high-grade lymphomas.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A highly aggressive germinal-center B-cell lymphoma that may involve the jaw or maxilla, particularly in endemic or immunodeficiency-associated settings. It typically shows a very high proliferation rate and MYC rearrangement.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal typ.description: An Epstein-Barr virus-associated aggressive lymphoma that can cause destructive lesions of the nasal cavity, palate, and maxilla, often with necrosis and ulceration.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption characterized by slowly enlarging annular or polycyclic red plaques, often with a characteristic trailing scale just inside the advancing edge.

Tinea corporis (extensive dermatophytosi.description: A superficial fungal infection of keratinized skin that produces expanding annular plaques with a more active scaly erythematous border and relative central clearing.

Erythema gyratum repens.description: A rare rapidly spreading figurate erythema with concentric, wood-grain-like erythematous bands and trailing scale; it can be associated with an underlying malignancy but may also occur in nonmalignant settings.

Annular psoriasis.description: A less common morphologic form of psoriasis in which erythematous plaques develop annular or circinate borders with scale, sometimes with central clearing.

Xanthogranulomatous gastritis.description: A rare benign chronic inflammatory disorder of the stomach characterized by infiltration of the gastric wall by lipid-laden foamy macrophages, chronic inflammatory cells, and fibrosis. It can form a mass-like lesion and mimic gastric cancer or a gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

Gastric malakoplakia.description: A rare granulomatous inflammatory condition caused by impaired macrophage bacterial killing, producing sheets of foamy histiocytes in the gastrointestinal tract. It may appear as a gastric mass or thickened folds and can resemble malignancy.

Diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma (linitis.normalized_text: Diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma (linitis plastica or infiltrative gastric carcinoma)
Diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma (linitis.description: An infiltrative gastric cancer that can produce diffuse wall thickening, distorted enlarged folds, reduced gastric compliance, and gastric outlet obstruction. Poorly differentiated tumors may be difficult to distinguish from inflammatory lesions on limited biopsy samples.

Inherited heterozygous genetic variant o.normalized_text: Inherited heterozygous genetic variant of uncertain clinical significance
Inherited heterozygous genetic variant o.description: The chromatogram appears to show a sequence variant in the child that may also be present in a parent, suggesting possible inheritance. Without the gene name, exact nucleotide change, zygosity interpretation, and clinical findings, the variant cannot be linked to a specific disease.

Benign familial genetic polymorphism.description: A DNA sequence difference inherited from a parent may represent a normal, non-disease-causing polymorphism rather than a pathogenic mutation.

Possible autosomal dominant genetic diso.normalized_text: Possible autosomal dominant genetic disorder, unspecified
Possible autosomal dominant genetic diso.description: If the sequencing trace represents a pathogenic heterozygous variant shared by an affected parent and child, an autosomal dominant condition could be possible. A specific disorder cannot be identified without knowing the tested gene, variant annotation, and clinical phenotype.

Acute ischemic stroke due to middle cere.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke due to middle cerebral artery occlusion
Acute ischemic stroke due to middle cere.description: An acute blockage of a middle cerebral artery causing reduced blood flow and early brain infarction in its vascular territory.

Acute right middle cerebral artery terri.normalized_text: Acute right middle cerebral artery territory infarction
Acute right middle cerebral artery terri.description: An acute cerebral infarct affecting brain tissue supplied by the right middle cerebral artery, commonly from thromboembolic arterial occlusion.

Cerebral venous thrombosis with cortical.normalized_text: Cerebral venous thrombosis with cortical venous congestion
Cerebral venous thrombosis with cortical.description: Thrombosis of cerebral veins or venous sinuses can produce hyperdense cortical venous structures and focal cerebral edema or infarction.

Extraosseous Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.normalized_text: Extraosseous Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor (pPNET)
Extraosseous Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.description: A malignant small round-cell sarcoma that can arise in soft tissues of the abdomen or mesentery. It commonly shows diffuse membranous CD99 expression and may show nuclear expression of markers such as FLI1 or NKX2.2.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor.description: A rare aggressive intra-abdominal small round-cell malignancy, usually arising from the peritoneum or mesentery. It often presents as an abdominal mass and typically expresses desmin, cytokeratins, and WT1.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the mesen.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the mesentery or gastrointestinal tract
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the mesen.description: A hematologic malignancy of lymphocytes that can form abdominal, mesenteric, or intestinal masses. Diagnosis is supported by lymphoid morphology and immunostaining for B-cell or T-cell markers.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis.description: A parasitic skin infection caused by Leishmania species, transmitted by sandflies. In Spain, Leishmania infantum is an important cause. Skin biopsy or smear may show macrophages containing intracellular amastigotes with kinetoplasts.

Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.description: A disseminated form of cutaneous leishmaniasis characterized by widespread non-ulcerated papules, nodules, plaques, or diffuse erythematous lesions and abundant parasites in macrophages. It is more likely in patients with impaired cellular immunity.

Cutaneous histoplasmosis.description: A fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that can produce skin lesions and intracellular yeast forms within macrophages. It is uncommon in Spain without travel to an endemic region and often occurs in immunocompromised individuals.
