Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A syndrome of sustained marked eosinophilia with eosinophil-mediated tissue or organ injury after exclusion of secondary causes, including parasites, drugs, allergic disease, autoimmune disease, and clonal hematologic neoplasms.

Reactive eosinophilia due to helminthic.normalized_text: Reactive eosinophilia due to helminthic parasitic infection, such as strongyloidiasis or toxocariasis
Reactive eosinophilia due to helminthic.description: Tissue-invasive helminth infections can produce eosinophilia, gastrointestinal inflammation, hepatic enzyme abnormalities, and occasionally eosinophilic infiltrates in involved tissues. Exposure history, stool testing, serology, and travel history are needed for confirmation.

Systemic mastocytosis with associated he.normalized_text: Systemic mastocytosis with associated hematologic neoplasm or another myeloid neoplasm with eosinophilia
Systemic mastocytosis with associated he.description: Systemic mast cell disease may coexist with a myeloid neoplasm and can cause eosinophilia, marrow abnormalities, hepatobiliary dysfunction, and constitutional or gastrointestinal manifestations. This diagnosis would require marrow mast-cell aggregates and appropriate immunophenotypic and molecular studies.

Hodgkin lymphoma or T-cell lymphoma with.normalized_text: Hodgkin lymphoma or T-cell lymphoma with paraneoplastic eosinophilia
Hodgkin lymphoma or T-cell lymphoma with.description: Some lymphomas, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma and certain T-cell lymphomas, can produce cytokines such as IL-5 that drive eosinophilia. These disorders generally cause lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, and less often severe leukemoid eosinophilia.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype.description: An aggressive diffuse astrocytic glioma, usually with necrosis, vascular proliferation, hemorrhage, marked edema, and ring enhancement. The immunoprofile shown is compatible with a glial tumor: GFAP and Olig2 positivity, absent IDH1 R132H staining, retained ATRX expression, p53 positivity, and increased proliferative activity.

Diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-wildtype with h.normalized_text: Diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-wildtype with high-grade features
Diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-wildtype with h.description: A diffusely infiltrating astrocytic tumor lacking the common IDH1 R132H mutation by immunohistochemistry. In an adult, an IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumor with necrosis, hemorrhage, ring enhancement, and high proliferation is generally biologically similar to glioblastoma.

Solitary brain metastasis.description: A metastatic systemic cancer deposit in the brain can present as a well-circumscribed ring-enhancing lesion with extensive vasogenic edema and intralesional hemorrhage. Certain metastases, such as melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, and choriocarcinoma, may bleed.

Cerebral abscess.description: A focal intracerebral infection containing purulent material, often producing a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding edema and mass effect. Diffusion restriction and clinical evidence of infection are usually important diagnostic clues.

Vertebral cryptococcosis.description: A fungal infection caused by Cryptococcus species that can disseminate from the lungs to bone, producing vertebral osteomyelitis and paravertebral soft-tissue masses, particularly in immunocompromised patients but occasionally in immunocompetent individuals.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with vertebr.description: Infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, usually acquired by inhalation. It may leave calcified pulmonary and mediastinal lymph-node granulomas and can disseminate to bone in susceptible patients.

Vertebral coccidioidomycosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Coccidioides species. Pulmonary infection can disseminate hematogenously to bone, including the spine, causing osteomyelitis, abscesses, and lytic vertebral lesions.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).description: Spinal infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, typically involving vertebral bodies and adjacent discs and often producing paravertebral abscesses. It may coexist with prior pulmonary or lymph-node tuberculosis.

Disseminated Lomentospora prolificans in.normalized_text: Disseminated Lomentospora prolificans infection (formerly Scedosporium prolificans)
Disseminated Lomentospora prolificans in.description: A severe opportunistic mold infection that can disseminate through the bloodstream, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It commonly involves the lungs, skin, soft tissues, bones, and central nervous system and is notable for frequent antifungal resistance. Spain is an area where this mold has been reported.

Disseminated scedosporiosis due to Scedo.normalized_text: Disseminated scedosporiosis due to Scedosporium apiospermum species complex
Disseminated scedosporiosis due to Scedo.description: Scedosporium species are environmental filamentous fungi that can cause pulmonary disease, subcutaneous infection, abscesses, and disseminated infection in susceptible individuals. Tissue microscopy typically shows septate branching hyphae.

Disseminated invasive aspergillosis.description: An opportunistic Aspergillus mold infection, most often occurring in people with severe immune suppression. It usually begins in the lungs and may spread to skin, soft tissue, brain, kidneys, or other organs; tissue commonly shows narrow septate acute-angle branching hyphae.

Disseminated mucormycosis.description: A life-threatening invasive infection caused by Mucorales molds. It can produce angioinvasive pulmonary disease and necrotic cutaneous or soft-tissue infection, especially in patients with diabetes, neutropenia, iron overload, or other major immune compromise. Histology typically demonstrates broad, ribbon-like sparsely septate hyphae.

Congenital Zika virus syndrome.description: Fetal abnormalities caused by maternal Zika virus infection during pregnancy, including central nervous system malformations, ventriculomegaly, abnormal corpus callosum or cavum septi pellucidi, calcifications, and sometimes microcephaly.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: A congenital viral infection acquired transplacentally that can cause fetal ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcifications, microcephaly, abnormal brain development, growth restriction, and later hearing loss.

Congenital toxoplasmosis.description: Transplacental infection with Toxoplasma gondii that may produce hydrocephalus or ventriculomegaly, diffuse intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, and neurologic impairment.

Isolated fetal ventriculomegaly due to n.normalized_text: Isolated fetal ventriculomegaly due to noninfectious cerebral malformation
Isolated fetal ventriculomegaly due to n.description: Ventricular enlargement may result from developmental brain abnormalities, genetic disorders, obstruction of cerebrospinal-fluid flow, or abnormalities of midline structures such as the corpus callosum or cavum septi pellucidi.

diagnoses.name: Complex hereditary spastic paraplegia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Autosomal recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia

Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11), also.normalized_text: Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11), also called hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin corpus callosum
Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11), also.description: An autosomal-recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SPG11. It commonly produces progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness, cognitive impairment, dysarthria, peripheral neuropathy, and thinning of the corpus callosum on brain MRI.

Complicated autosomal-recessive heredita.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive corticospinal-tract dysfunction causing spastic paraparesis. Complicated forms additionally involve cognitive impairment, dysarthria, neuropathy, ataxia, seizures, or characteristic brain-imaging abnormalities.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin corpus callosum (HSP-TCC phenotype)
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin.description: A clinical-radiologic syndrome of complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia featuring spastic paraparesis with a thin corpus callosum, cognitive impairment, and white-matter abnormalities. SPG11 is the most frequent genetic cause.

Cardiac paraganglioma.description: A rare, highly vascular neuroendocrine tumor arising from paraganglionic tissue, often located near the atrioventricular grooves or great vessels. These tumors may show intense FDG uptake and avid contrast enhancement on cardiac imaging.

Primary cardiac lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid tumor involving the heart, most often affecting the right atrium, right ventricle, pericardium, or atrioventricular groove. It is typically strongly FDG-avid.

Primary cardiac angiosarcoma.description: An aggressive malignant vascular tumor of the heart that most commonly arises in the right atrium and can demonstrate FDG uptake and contrast enhancement due to its vascular nature.

Nocardia brain abscess.description: A focal central nervous system infection caused by Nocardia species, aerobic Gram-positive branching bacteria that can produce multiloculated abscesses and may disseminate from the lungs or skin.

Pyogenic bacterial brain abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in the brain caused by bacteria, commonly producing a ring-enhancing lesion with central restricted diffusion and surrounding vasogenic edema.

Actinomyces cerebral abscess.description: An uncommon chronic bacterial infection caused by Actinomyces species, anaerobic or microaerophilic Gram-positive branching rods that can occasionally form intracranial abscesses.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis.description: An opportunistic infection caused by Toxoplasma gondii that commonly produces multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions, particularly in people with advanced HIV infection or other severe immunosuppression.

Glioblastoma or other necrotic high-grad.normalized_text: Glioblastoma or other necrotic high-grade glioma
Glioblastoma or other necrotic high-grad.description: A malignant primary brain tumor that can show irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, edema, and mass effect, sometimes mimicking an abscess on imaging.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: A severe atypical bacterial pneumonia caused by Legionella, often acquired by inhaling aerosolized water from lakes, spas, cooling systems, or plumbing.

Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.description: An acute infection of the lung parenchyma caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, or gram-negative organisms.

Atypical pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pne.normalized_text: Atypical pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Chlamydia pneumoniae
Atypical pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pne.description: Respiratory infection caused by atypical bacteria that can produce patchy, bilateral, and sometimes progressive pulmonary infiltrates.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis related to.normalized_text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis related to environmental water or mold exposure
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis related to.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory lung disease caused by inhaled environmental antigens, including molds or aerosolized organisms from damp buildings or water exposures.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to MU.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to MUSK mutation
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to MU.description: A hereditary neuromuscular-junction disorder caused by impaired muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) signaling, leading to defective acetylcholine-receptor clustering, immature postsynaptic folds, and impaired neuromuscular transmission.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to AG.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to AGRN mutation
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to AG.description: A congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by deficient agrin signaling. Agrin is required for normal formation and maintenance of the neuromuscular junction and acetylcholine-receptor clustering.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to LR.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to LRP4 mutation
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to LR.description: A hereditary disorder of neuromuscular-junction development caused by defective LRP4, an agrin receptor that activates MuSK and promotes acetylcholine-receptor clustering and synaptic maturation.

Acetylcholine receptor deficiency congen.normalized_text: Acetylcholine receptor deficiency congenital myasthenic syndrome
Acetylcholine receptor deficiency congen.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome, often caused by mutations in acetylcholine-receptor subunit genes such as CHRNE, resulting in reduced functional acetylcholine receptors at the endplate.

RAPSN-related congenital myasthenic synd.description: A congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by rapsyn deficiency, impairing clustering and stabilization of acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic membrane.

Calcium oxalate crystalluria / possible.normalized_text: Calcium oxalate crystalluria / possible calcium oxalate kidney stones
Calcium oxalate crystalluria / possible.description: Calcium oxalate crystals are common urinary sediment crystals and may appear as envelope-shaped, oval, dumbbell-shaped, or elongated forms. They can be seen in people with kidney stones or occasionally in otherwise healthy individuals.

Dehydration with concentrated urine.description: Low fluid intake or increased fluid loss can concentrate urine and promote visible urinary crystals, including calcium oxalate, uric acid, or phosphate crystals.

Hyperoxaluria.description: Hyperoxaluria is excess oxalate excretion in urine, which can increase calcium oxalate crystal formation and predispose to recurrent kidney stones. It may result from diet, intestinal malabsorption, supplements, or rare inherited disorders.

Internal jugular vein thrombosis.description: Thrombus formation within the internal jugular vein, often appearing on contrast CT as an enlarged vein with an intraluminal filling defect or reduced contrast opacification.

Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal.normalized_text: Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein (Lemierre syndrome)
Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal.description: A potentially severe infection-associated thrombosis of the internal jugular vein, classically following pharyngitis or tonsillitis and often caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum.

Noninfectious thrombosis of the internal.normalized_text: Noninfectious thrombosis of the internal jugular vein related to hypercoagulability, malignancy, catheter use, or local compression
Noninfectious thrombosis of the internal.description: Internal jugular venous thrombosis can occur without infection because of a central venous catheter, cancer, inherited/acquired thrombophilia, trauma, surgery, or compression by a neighboring mass.

Internal jugular vein compression or inv.normalized_text: Internal jugular vein compression or invasion by a cervical mass/lymphadenopathy
Internal jugular vein compression or inv.description: A neck mass, metastatic lymph node, inflammatory lesion, or thyroid lesion can compress the internal jugular vein and cause impaired venous flow, sometimes leading to secondary thrombosis.

Celiac disease.description: Immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten, causing small-intestinal mucosal inflammation, villous injury, and malabsorption. The biopsy appearance is compatible with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and villous/crypt architectural abnormalities.

Refractory celiac disease.description: Persistent or recurrent celiac-type enteropathy despite a strict gluten-free diet; it can be associated with marked small-bowel inflammation, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, ulceration, and risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.

Giardiasis.description: Infection of the upper small intestine by Giardia duodenalis, a protozoan parasite that may cause duodenitis, malabsorption, and occasionally celiac-like biopsy findings.

Whipple disease.description: A rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that often affects the small intestine and may produce malabsorption, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and characteristic macrophage-rich intestinal biopsies.

Aerococcus urinae infection.description: An infection caused by Aerococcus urinae, a Gram-positive coccus that commonly appears in clusters or tetrads and may produce small alpha-hemolytic colonies on blood agar. It is most often associated with urinary tract infection, bacteremia, and occasionally endocarditis, particularly in older adults with urinary tract abnormalities.

Aerococcus viridans infection.description: Aerococcus viridans is a Gram-positive, catalase-negative coccus that can resemble staphylococci microscopically because it forms clusters or tetrads. It can cause opportunistic urinary, bloodstream, wound, or endocardial infections.

Staphylococcus epidermidis infection.description: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative Gram-positive coccus that forms clusters and commonly produces white to gray, usually nonhemolytic colonies. It is a frequent skin contaminant but can cause genuine infection involving intravascular catheters, prosthetic devices, and other implanted materials.

Micrococcus species infection or coloniz.description: Micrococcus species are Gram-positive cocci that often occur in tetrads or irregular clusters. They are usually harmless skin commensals or contaminants but can rarely cause opportunistic bloodstream infection in immunocompromised patients or those with invasive devices.

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type

Hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.description: A rare vascular tumor of the liver that often presents with multiple peripheral hepatic lesions and may spread to the lungs, lymph nodes, peritoneum, or bone.

Metastatic malignancy to the liver, poss.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy to the liver, possibly from an occult primary tumor
Metastatic malignancy to the liver, poss.description: Cancer spread to the liver from another primary site can produce multiple liver lesions and may coexist with lung, nodal, peritoneal, or skeletal metastases.

Hepatic sarcoidosis with pulmonary sarco.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that commonly affects the lungs and can produce multiple small hypodense hepatic lesions and abdominal lymphadenopathy.

Disseminated lymphoma with hepatic and p.normalized_text: Disseminated lymphoma with hepatic and pulmonary involvement
Disseminated lymphoma with hepatic and p.description: Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve the liver, lungs, lymph nodes, spleen, and retroperitoneum, producing multiple low-attenuation lesions and PET-avid disease.

Partial anomalous pulmonary venous retur.normalized_text: Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR), left-sided vertical vein variant
Partial anomalous pulmonary venous retur.description: A congenital cardiovascular anomaly in which one or more pulmonary veins drain into a systemic vein rather than the left atrium; left upper pulmonary venous drainage into the left brachiocephalic vein through a vertical vein is a recognized pattern.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (PA.description: An abnormal direct communication between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein that creates a right-to-left shunt and may appear as enlarged tortuous pulmonary feeding and draining vessels on contrast imaging.

Pulmonary sequestration with anomalous s.normalized_text: Pulmonary sequestration with anomalous systemic arterial supply
Pulmonary sequestration with anomalous s.description: A congenital lung malformation in which a portion of lung tissue receives systemic arterial blood, commonly from the descending thoracic aorta, rather than from the pulmonary artery; it may be associated with abnormal vessels visible on CT angiography.

Pulmonary vein varix or pulmonary venous.normalized_text: Pulmonary vein varix or pulmonary venous aneurysm
Pulmonary vein varix or pulmonary venous.description: A localized congenital or acquired dilatation of a pulmonary vein that can mimic a pulmonary hilar mass or vascular malformation and is best characterized with contrast-enhanced CT angiography.

Acute mesenteric venous thrombosis with.normalized_text: Acute mesenteric venous thrombosis with mesenteric ischemia
Acute mesenteric venous thrombosis with.description: Thrombosis of the superior mesenteric vein or its branches can impair venous drainage from the bowel, causing mesenteric edema, bowel-wall edema, ascites, and potentially intestinal infarction.

Acute small-bowel ischemia.description: Reduced intestinal blood flow, due to arterial occlusion, venous thrombosis, or low-flow states, may produce bowel-wall thickening, mesenteric edema, dilated bowel loops, and later pneumatosis or infarction.

Infectious or inflammatory enteritis.description: Inflammation of the small intestine from infection, inflammatory bowel disease, medication-related injury, or other causes can lead to bowel-wall thickening, hyperemia, mesenteric edema, and abdominal fluid.

Large left pneumothorax.description: Air in the left pleural space causing partial or near-complete collapse of the left lung. The radiograph shows marked left-sided hyperlucency with reduced/absent peripheral lung markings.

Tension pneumothorax.description: A life-threatening form of pneumothorax in which pleural air accumulates under pressure, potentially compressing the lung and shifting mediastinal structures.

Giant pulmonary bulla (bullous emphysema.description: A large air-filled space within the lung caused by destruction of alveolar tissue, which can mimic a pneumothorax on chest radiography.

Rheumatic mitral stenosis.description: Narrowing of the mitral valve, most often from chronic rheumatic valve scarring, causing impaired blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle and elevated left-atrial pressure.

Mitral regurgitation.description: Leakage of blood backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole, caused by primary mitral-valve disease or functional distortion of the valve apparatus.

Mixed rheumatic mitral valve disease (mi.normalized_text: Mixed rheumatic mitral valve disease (mitral stenosis with mitral regurgitation)
Mixed rheumatic mitral valve disease (mi.description: Combined narrowing and incompetence of the mitral valve, commonly due to rheumatic heart disease; it can produce both turbulent diastolic inflow and systolic regurgitant flow.

Lumbar spondylodiscitis with epidural ab.description: Infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral endplates, which can extend into the epidural space and compress the thecal sac or nerve roots.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).description: Spinal infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, typically affecting adjacent vertebral bodies with paraspinal or epidural abscess formation and sometimes relatively preserved disc height early in disease.

Brucellar spondylodiscitis.description: Brucella infection of the spine, commonly involving the lumbar region and causing vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis; it is relevant in Mediterranean countries, including Spain.

Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis due to.normalized_text: Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis due to Staphylococcus aureus or other bacteria
Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis due to.description: A bacterial infection of vertebral bone and disc space, often caused by hematogenous spread of Staphylococcus aureus, with potential formation of epidural and paraspinal abscesses.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis.description: A parasitic skin infection transmitted by sand flies; in Spain it is commonly caused by Leishmania infantum. It may produce a chronic papule, nodule, or ulcer with crusting and regional lymph-node enlargement.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of keratinizing skin cells that can present as a persistent scaly, crusted, ulcerated, or nonhealing lesion, particularly on sun-exposed facial skin.

Basal cell carcinoma.description: A slow-growing skin cancer most often occurring on sun-exposed areas of the face. It may appear as a pearly papule, nonhealing sore, or ulcer with crusting.

Bacterial infection of the oral commissu.normalized_text: Bacterial infection of the oral commissure (ecthyma or impetiginized angular cheilitis)
Bacterial infection of the oral commissu.description: A superficial or deeper bacterial skin infection, often involving Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus species, which can cause erosions, ulcers, and yellow-brown crusting around the mouth.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.description: An inherited hamartomatous polyposis syndrome characterized by multiple gastrointestinal polyps, especially in the small intestine, which can act as lead points for intussusception and bowel obstruction.

Juvenile polyposis syndrome.description: A hereditary hamartomatous polyposis disorder causing multiple juvenile-type polyps, usually in the colon and stomach, with possible gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, and obstruction.

Familial adenomatous polyposis.description: An inherited APC-associated syndrome with numerous adenomatous polyps, primarily in the colon and rectum, and increased risk of colorectal and upper gastrointestinal cancer.

Dupuytren disease (palmar fibromatosis).description: A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia that forms nodules and cords, progressively pulling one or more fingers into flexion contracture, most often the ring and little fingers.

Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosyn.description: Inflammation and thickening around the flexor tendon pulley that causes painful catching, locking, or fixed flexion of a finger.

Camptodactyly.description: A congenital or developmental condition characterized by a painless flexion contracture, usually at the proximal interphalangeal joint and commonly affecting the little finger.

Post-traumatic flexion contracture of th.normalized_text: Post-traumatic flexion contracture of the finger
Post-traumatic flexion contracture of th.description: Loss of finger extension resulting from previous injury, scarring, immobilization, tendon injury, or joint capsular contracture.

Rheumatoid arthritis with hand deformity.description: A chronic inflammatory autoimmune arthritis that can cause pain, swelling, stiffness, tendon imbalance, and progressive finger deformities.

Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae.description: A zoonotic infection caused by Bartonella henselae, usually transmitted through a cat scratch, bite, or flea exposure. It commonly causes regional painful lymphadenopathy with necrotizing/suppurative granulomatous lymphadenitis; organisms may be demonstrated with Warthin-Starry stain or immunohistochemistry.

Tularemia (Francisella tularensis lympha.description: Tularemia is a zoonotic infection acquired through ticks, animal contact, or contaminated environmental exposure. The ulceroglandular form can produce regional lymphadenopathy with suppurative granulomas and necrosis.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia trac.description: Lymphogranuloma venereum is a sexually transmitted invasive Chlamydia infection that can cause painful unilateral or bilateral inguinal and femoral lymphadenopathy, sometimes with suppuration and buboes.

Nonspecific bacterial suppurative lympha.description: Acute bacterial infection of a draining lymph node, commonly due to skin or soft-tissue pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. It produces painful lymph node enlargement with neutrophilic inflammation and possible abscess formation.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis.description: Tuberculous lymphadenitis is infection of lymph nodes by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually causing chronic painless lymph node enlargement with granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis.

diagnoses.icd11_title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

Malignant pleural mesothelioma.description: An aggressive cancer arising from pleural mesothelial cells, often producing unilateral pleural effusion, diffuse pleural thickening, and pleural nodules or masses.

Metastatic pleural carcinomatosis.description: Spread of a cancer from another organ, commonly lung, breast, ovary, gastrointestinal tract, or kidney, to the pleura; it can cause pleural nodules, thickening, and malignant pleural effusion.

Primary lung adenocarcinoma with pleural.normalized_text: Primary lung adenocarcinoma with pleural involvement
Primary lung adenocarcinoma with pleural.description: A common type of non-small-cell lung cancer that may invade the pleura or seed the pleural space, resulting in malignant effusion and pleural nodules.

Pleural tuberculosis.description: Infection of the pleura by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which can cause a predominantly unilateral exudative pleural effusion and pleural thickening; chronic disease may produce nodularity.

Splenic coccidioidomycosis.description: A fungal infection caused by Coccidioides species. Tissue examination may show large thick-walled spherules containing endospores, and disseminated disease can involve the spleen, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

Splenic blastomycosis.description: Blastomycosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by Blastomyces species. It can disseminate beyond the lungs and may produce broad-based budding yeast forms in cytologic or histologic specimens.

Splenic paracoccidioidomycosis.description: Paracoccidioidomycosis is a chronic systemic fungal infection caused by Paracoccidioides species. Histology can show multiple budding yeast cells with a characteristic pilot-wheel appearance and may involve reticuloendothelial organs including the spleen.

Visceral leishmaniasis with splenic invo.description: Visceral leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection caused by Leishmania species and is endemic in parts of Spain. It typically causes splenomegaly and may be diagnosed by demonstrating intracellular amastigotes in macrophages from splenic or bone-marrow samples.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiom.normalized_text: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), also called arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiom.description: An inherited cardiomyopathy in which right-ventricular myocardium is progressively replaced by fibrofatty tissue, causing right-ventricular dilation, dysfunction, ventricular arrhythmias, and risk of sudden cardiac death.

Uhl anomaly.description: A rare congenital disorder characterized by marked absence or severe thinning of right-ventricular myocardium, producing a dilated, poorly contractile right ventricle. It can resemble ARVC but usually reflects a congenital structural abnormality rather than fibrofatty myocardial replacement.

Right ventricular outflow tract ventricu.normalized_text: Right ventricular outflow tract ventricular tachycardia (RVOT-VT)
Right ventricular outflow tract ventricu.description: A usually idiopathic ventricular arrhythmia originating in the right-ventricular outflow tract, commonly causing palpitations and monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block-like ECG morphology.

Acute ischemic stroke in the middle cere.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke in the middle cerebral artery territory
Acute ischemic stroke in the middle cere.description: An acute cerebral infarction caused by reduced or blocked arterial blood flow, suggested by focal diffusion-restricted brain lesions on MRI.

Intracranial atherosclerotic disease wit.normalized_text: Intracranial atherosclerotic disease with recurrent ischemic infarction
Intracranial atherosclerotic disease wit.description: Narrowing or occlusion of intracranial arteries due to atherosclerotic plaque can produce recurrent territorial or small deep infarcts.

Moyamoya disease or moyamoya syndrome.description: A progressive narrowing of the terminal internal carotid and proximal cerebral arteries that causes collateral vessel formation and recurrent ischemic strokes.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: Inflammation of cerebral blood vessels that can cause multifocal arterial narrowing and ischemic strokes of differing ages.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often causing arterial wall thickening, stenosis, aneurysmal dilation, aortic regurgitation, and systemic inflammation.

Infectious aortitis with aortic valve en.normalized_text: Infectious aortitis with aortic valve endocarditis
Infectious aortitis with aortic valve en.description: Infection of the aortic wall, sometimes associated with infective endocarditis, can produce intense inflammation, aortic wall abnormalities, aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm formation, and severe aortic regurgitation.

Giant cell arteritis with aortitis.description: A granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis that usually affects older adults and may involve the thoracic aorta, causing aortitis, aneurysmal dilation, dissection risk, and occasionally aortic-valve regurgitation.

Behcet disease with large-vessel vasculi.description: A multisystem inflammatory vasculitis that can affect arteries and veins of all sizes. Large-vessel involvement may cause aortitis, aneurysms, arterial thrombosis, pulmonary vascular disease, and valvular or aortic-root complications.

IgG4-related aortitis/periaortitis.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder that can cause aortic wall thickening, periaortic soft tissue, aneurysmal disease, and involvement of multiple organs such as the pancreas, salivary glands, kidneys, and retroperitoneum.

Adult midgut volvulus.description: Twisting of the small-bowel mesentery around the superior mesenteric vessels, usually associated with congenital intestinal malrotation. CT may show a mesenteric 'whirlpool' sign.

Intestinal malrotation with Ladd bands.description: A congenital abnormality of intestinal rotation and fixation that can remain undiagnosed until adulthood and predispose to midgut volvulus or intermittent bowel obstruction.

Internal hernia with small-bowel volvulu.description: Herniation of bowel through a mesenteric or peritoneal defect can produce clustered bowel loops and twisting of mesenteric vessels, potentially causing obstruction or ischemia.

Splenic hydatid cyst (splenic echinococc.description: Parasitic infection caused by Echinococcus species producing a slowly enlarging cyst in the spleen. It is an important consideration in Mediterranean regions including Spain.

Primary nonparasitic splenic cyst (epide.normalized_text: Primary nonparasitic splenic cyst (epidermoid/congenital splenic cyst)
Primary nonparasitic splenic cyst (epide.description: A benign true cyst of the spleen, often congenital and lined by epithelium. It may become very large and can contain internal echoes from proteinaceous material or hemorrhage.

Splenic pseudocyst.description: A nonparasitic splenic cyst without an epithelial lining, usually occurring after prior splenic trauma, hematoma, infarction, or infection. Chronic lesions may contain debris, calcification, or complex fluid.

Splenic abscess.description: A localized collection of infected fluid in the spleen, usually related to bloodstream infection, immunosuppression, trauma, or spread from another infection. Ultrasound may show a complex cystic mass with internal debris.

Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.description: A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome caused by a deletion at chromosome 11p11.2, typically involving EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It is characterized by multiple osteochondromas, enlarged parietal foramina, craniofacial differences, and variable developmental delay or intellectual disability.

Hereditary multiple osteochondromas (mul.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, usually caused by pathogenic variants in EXT1 or EXT2, resulting in multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near the metaphyses of long bones.

ALX4-related enlarged parietal foramina.description: A genetic skull ossification disorder caused by altered ALX4 function, producing persistent enlarged openings in the parietal bones due to incomplete intramembranous ossification.

Cleidocranial dysplasia.description: A skeletal dysplasia caused by RUNX2-related impaired bone formation, classically featuring delayed closure of cranial sutures/fontanelles, clavicular hypoplasia, dental abnormalities, and short stature.

Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei infestation).description: A contagious skin infestation caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, which burrows into the stratum corneum and causes intense inflammation, itching, papules, excoriations, and sometimes ulcerated lesions.

Crusted scabies.description: A severe form of scabies with a very high mite burden, often producing extensive crusting, hyperkeratosis, erosions, ulceration, and widespread inflammatory lesions. It is more likely in people with impaired immunity, neurologic disease, disability, or inability to scratch.

Scabies with secondary bacterial infecti.normalized_text: Scabies with secondary bacterial infection (impetiginized scabies)
Scabies with secondary bacterial infecti.description: Scabies lesions may become secondarily infected, commonly with Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, producing painful erosions, ulceration, crusting, purulent drainage, or impetigo-like lesions.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.description: An immune-complex-mediated kidney disease characterized by mesangial proliferation, lobulated glomeruli, and thickening or duplication of glomerular capillary walls.

IgA nephropathy.description: A common immune-mediated glomerulonephritis caused by mesangial deposition of IgA, often producing mesangial hypercellularity and recurrent blood in the urine.

Lupus nephritis.description: Kidney inflammation caused by systemic lupus erythematosus, often producing proliferative glomerular lesions with marked mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity.

Crescentic glomerulonephritis / rapidly.description: A severe form of glomerular inflammation that can cause rapid loss of kidney function and may show extracapillary cellular proliferation (crescents) on biopsy.

Eosinophilic cholangitis.description: A rare benign inflammatory disorder characterized by dense eosinophil infiltration of the bile ducts, producing biliary wall thickening, strictures, and obstruction that may mimic cholangiocarcinoma.

Cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor arising from bile duct epithelium, commonly presenting as a hilar or intrahepatic biliary stricture with upstream bile duct dilatation.

IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disease causing bile duct wall thickening and strictures, often associated with autoimmune pancreatitis and increased IgG4-positive plasma cells.

Hepatobiliary fascioliasis.description: Infection with the liver fluke Fasciola hepatica, which is encountered in parts of Spain and can cause eosinophilic hepatic inflammation, biliary obstruction, and cholangitis.
